  makes to the thing's id. Then a second run finds it and does not make
  another.

A webhook is a message another system sends to your server when something
happens. For systems that push like this, add a `webhook_triggers` entry.
It names a **verification profile**: Stripe, GitHub, Telegram, Slack,
Paddle, Lemon Squeezy, or a generic token / HMAC / basic-auth mechanism. The
endpoint checks the signature before your recipe ever fires. Then the
recipe reads the accepted event body.

Do not check the signature again inside the recipe. That already happened
at the door. Do treat the body as untrusted data. Gate on the fields you
need. Skip when they are missing. Webhooks POST straight to your server.
Nothing is passed through anyone's cloud.

When there is no event source, a recipe can tick by itself. It gates each
tick:

```json
"auto_run": { "interval_ms": 3600000 },
"trigger_steps": [
  { "id": "window", "op": "core.watch.time",
    "args": { "weekdays": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], "start_hour": 7, "end_hour": 19 } }
]
```

Every trigger step must return `should_run: true`. If not, the tick passes
quietly.

section: Gating a tick without an extra call
body:
There are built-in watch operations. There are also these transforms. They
answer "has this changed?" from data you already fetched. So a gate costs
no extra call:

| Transform | Answers |
| --- | --- |
| `time_within_window` | Is now inside the allowed hours and weekdays? `now`, `weekdays?`, `start_hour?`, `end_hour?` |
| `time_elapsed_since` | Has `window_ms` passed since `since_ms`? |
| `mail_received` | Did any mail arrive that matches `from` / `subject` / `label`? |
| `file_changed` | Did any file under `path_prefix` change since `since_ms`? |
| `calendar_new_since` | Were events created since `since_ms`? |
| `calendar_changed_since` | Were events edited since `since_ms`? |
| `calendar_starting_soon` | Does an event start within `minutes_ahead`? |
| `attendee_diff` | Who joined or left, between an old and a new attendee list? |
| `http_changed` | Did an ETag or content hash change since last time? |
| `recipe_succeeded_since` | Has a given recipe already succeeded since `since_ms`? Use it to avoid doing work twice |

Each one returns the decision plus what it matched. So the same step gates
the tick and hands the detail to the steps after it.

Pick the slowest interval the job can live with. For a daily job, the
normal choice is an hourly tick gated by a morning window. And stop your
own repeats. A watcher may see the same thing on two ticks in a row. So it
must stamp what it acted on. Use an annotation on the record, or a marker
row. Do not trust the interval alone.

A run with nobody watching works out its settings in layers. First, the
recipe's variable defaults. Then the settings saved at install. Then the
schedule's or trigger's own settings. Each armed row can carry its own.
Write your variables so a run on pure defaults either works or stops and
asks for setup. It must never half-run.

Order your gates from cheap to costly. Put fixed checks before AI. Stop
safely at every step:

1. **Identity.** Is this event about the thing you watch? Cannot tell?
   Skip.
2. **State and window.** Is the watch still on? Is the time window open?
3. **Cheap fields.** Subject words, status, thresholds. Check these before
   any body read or vendor call.
4. **The costly read.** Only after the cheap gates pass.
5. **A purpose check on what you fetched.** Fixed rules, from words the user
   set up. Not sure? Record it for review and notify. Do not go on.
6. **AI last.** Only to summarize or classify. Only after privacy protection.
   Never as the thing that decides whether an action happens.

section: Keep outward actions out of unattended runs
body:
Some actions reach outside or are hard to undo. Sending mail. Posting
messages. Making events with other people on them. The strong pattern for
these is a split:

- The **unattended recipe detects**. It reads, works things out, writes a
  proposal, and notifies you.
- A **second recipe acts**. You run it yourself. From the notification, or
  from a `button` on a review digest. Running it is the decision. Its
  writes still pass [grants and approvals](../concepts/grants-and-approvals.md)
  like any other run.

A background run has nobody at the keyboard. At best, an outward action
waits as a held approval. At worst, a write with a wide grant happens with
no one looking. With the detect-then-act split, background work only piles
up proposals. You review them with context. You do not get asks, or
surprises.

- Events over polling when the source is synced. Read the payload's record
  again before use. Use the `prev is_null` gate on update subscriptions, but
  never on a mail fact trigger.
- Mail facts: one kind in `on`, unless any kind will do. `where` values
  written as the fact stores them. No template id in a recipe you publish.
- Webhooks: the profile checks the signature at the door. Steps gate on
  body fields.
- Watchers: the slowest interval you can live with. Repeats stopped with a
  stamp.
- Works on defaults, or stops and asks for setup.
- Gates ordered cheap → costly → AI. AI never gates an action.
- Nothing that reaches outside in the unattended path. Detect, propose,
  notify. Act in a recipe the owner runs.
- The description says what arms it, what fires it, and what it will never
  do.

Everything that reaches your server from outside comes in through a door. A
door is a way in that you open on purpose. Every door leads to the same gate.
The gate marks who is asking, checks the grants, and writes the audit diary.
This page goes app by app. Pick the thing you are connecting. Follow its
shape.

MCP is a shared language that AI apps use to call your server's tools.
Claude Desktop, Cursor, a custom agent, or a peer Recued can connect over
MCP:

1. Open the MCP door. Choose the tools it may show. The door makes its own
   secret key.
2. Give the agent your server's MCP address and that secret key.
3. The agent's calls arrive marked with its name. They pass your grants.
   They land in the audit diary.

The agent sees only what the door grants: warehouse reads, timelines, and
recipes as tools. Close the door, and its secret key stops working.

A peer Recued connects the same way, with one extra. Its owner can put a
question to you and hold their own run until you answer. See
[Ask a peer](asking-a-peer.md).

Some chat apps let you type in a custom base URL and an API key. Any app like
that can talk to a Recued server that has given it access. The app does not
need MCP. This is the way a seller's customers use an "ask my operated
knowledge" product. It speaks the standard shape:

- **Base URL**: your server's gateway address.
- **API key**: the door's secret key. The app sends it as a normal bearer key,
  which is a secret key sent with each request. Customers get theirs through
  a claim link.
- **`GET /v1/models`**: returns one model. Its name is an alias the server
  owner picks (`recued-seller` by default). The alias is only a label, not a
  choice. The server decides which real model answers. Its owner sets that.
- **`POST /v1/chat/completions`**: one request is one chat turn, and the gate
  checks it.

A turn runs on the server's chat engine. Answers come from what the connected
contract grants. A contract is the saved list of what one actor may do.
Granted recipes can be called as tools. They follow the same approval rules
as everything else. The privacy alias rule applies too. Known names, emails,
phone numbers, and addresses are swapped for placeholder aliases before text
leaves for the model. Your chat history
stays in your own app. The server does not mix it into the owner's chat
history.

section: Streaming, and what the gateway is not
body:
Two things to know. Streaming works: set `stream: true` and the answer comes
back as chunks, the way OpenAI sends them. The whole turn still runs first,
and the gate still checks it. While it runs, the gateway keeps the connection
open with small keep-alive lines, so a long turn does not time out. Then it
sends the answer in pieces. Ask for `stream_options.include_usage` and you
also get the token counts at the end. And expect chat completions only. This
is a chat surface. It is not a full copy of the OpenAI platform.

Slack and Telegram connect as messenger doors. Messages and slash commands
POST straight to your server. They never go through Recued's cloud. Replies,
notifications, and approvals can reach you in the same channel.

The webclient and the Browser Bridge do not come in through doors. They pair.
Pairing links a device to your server. It is a narrower, more trusted link. It
is only for machines you own. See
[Pairing and devices](../setup/pairing-and-devices.md).

No matter which app it is, the same things hold. The caller has a name. Its
access is exactly what its door or contract grants. Every call is written in
the audit diary. Rate and usage limits apply where the door sets them. And
taking access back is one action: close the door, or issue a new secret key.

- [AI chat and MCP](ai-chat-and-mcp.md): the built-in chat, and why it stays
  safe.
- [Selling access](selling-access.md): giving outsiders access in tiers, on
  your own terms.
- [Grants and approvals](../concepts/grants-and-approvals.md): the gate behind
  every door.

A connection is a saved way to talk to an outside service. It has a name.
The service can be an API, like your CRM. It can be an MCP tool server. It
can be a place that gets your notifications. Your server talks out to it.

A pack asks to use a connection by its name. You set up the secret key once.
Then any pack you grant it to reuses it. The key is never copied into a
recipe.

Enroll means "set up and save". Open **Settings → Connections** and pick a
provider. Or let a pack do it. A pack that needs a connection walks you
through the setup while it installs.

Each connection is known by its kind and its name. So `acme-hubspot` and
`personal-hubspot` are two different connections. Each one has its own
grants. A grant is a yes you give ahead of time.

section: CRM vendors bring their own app
body:
HubSpot and Salesforce work a bit differently. First you make an app inside
your own vendor account. For HubSpot, that is a developer app. For
Salesforce, that is a Connected App. Salesforce also has a sandbox switch.

Recued's cloud only gives you one static OAuth callback page. Your server
does the token swap. Your server stores the tokens. There is no central
place that holds everyone's tokens.

After you enroll, Recued checks what the provider really allowed. For
HubSpot, it checks the granted scopes. For Salesforce, it probes which
objects it can see. Is something missing? You see a warning on the
capability that needs it. A capability is one thing a pack can do. Nothing
is hidden.

A credential is a secret, like a key or a token. It stays on your server. Only the connection
executor uses it, and only at the moment of a call. A recipe can read the
non-secret fields of a connection. The secret key never goes into recipe
data or step outputs.

- CRM records in [the warehouse](../concepts/warehouse.md). Your server
  checks them against the vendor and fixes differences. Webhooks or
  streaming make that faster.
- Outgoing notifications. For example, sending email to many people through
  one named target.
- MCP tool servers that your recipes can call.

A mail account says whether it can send. A recipe checks that before it
tries to send. The server checks again at the moment it sends. A guard also
refuses mail sent from an address to that same address, so it cannot loop.
Outgoing mail goes from your server straight to your mail provider. It never
goes through Recued's cloud.

A recipe points at a connection by its name. If you delete that connection,
the things that need it stop working. They work again when you enroll a
connection with the same name. Grants attach to installed packs. So you can
change what a pack may do without setting up the secret key again.

- [Connect Gmail and Google Calendar](../setup/connect-google.md). Which way
  keeps working for your kind of Google account.
- [Connect Outlook and Microsoft 365](../setup/connect-microsoft.md). Who
  makes the sign-in app for your kind of Microsoft account.
- [Grants and approvals](../concepts/grants-and-approvals.md). How your
  server checks each granted action when it runs.

An exposed recipe shows up in the tool catalog. The built-in chat and every
connected agent read that catalog. The model sees only three things when it
picks a tool: the name, the description, and the variables. Exposing is a
choice about where the recipe is offered. It is the same recipe. It still
runs from the panel, from a schedule, or from a trigger, just like before.

Set `chat_exposed: true` on purpose. Recipes you wrote yourself on this
server are offered to chat by default. Recipes installed from packs stay
hidden unless the author turned them on. Every exposed entry makes the catalog
longer, and the model must read all of it. So expose recipe by recipe, not
all at once.

Expose a recipe when all three of these are true:

1. The job is something you would ask for in words. "What is overdue?"
   "Draft the intro." "Watch for the quote from Peter."
2. It runs from its arguments alone. It needs no page context. It needs
   nothing the model cannot give it.
3. It is the starting point of its workflow.

Keep these hidden: silent producers, the reactive half of a watcher pair, and
cleanup tools. A silent producer is a recipe that quietly makes facts for
other recipes. Also hide acting recipes that only make sense when started
from a proposal or a review. Never hand a model a lever when it cannot see
what must be true first. A workflow with many recipes usually exposes two:
its starting recipe and its review recipe. Nothing else.

section: Arguments: flat and easy to read
body:
Chat fills in `variables` like flags on a command line. Keep them flat:
single values, true/false, and lists. Never an object that hides the real
shape:

```json
"variables": {
  "expected_sender_email": { "label": "Sender email", "type": "string" },
  "subject_contains_any": { "label": "Subject terms", "type": "array",
                            "default": [] },
  "acct": { "label": "Accounting connection", "type": "connection",
            "connection_kind": "api", "default": "" }
}
```

Give everything a label. Add `help` when a value has a set format. A value
with no `optional` and no `default` is a must-have. Use that shape only for
true must-haves. Give the rest defaults that work. (There is no `required`
field. Recued refuses it when you install.) A call on
pure defaults should work, or it should stop with a clear message. It should
never half-run. And do not ask for raw vendor record ids as arguments if the
recipe can find them itself. It can find them from something a person knows,
like an email or a date range. The model rarely has ids.

section: Write the description so the model picks right
body:
The model chooses between many tools using only the name and description.

- Name the recipe with a verb, and be specific:
  `audit-subscriptions-from-mail`, not `subscription-helper`.
- Say what it reads and what it never does. "Read-only; never sends or
  deletes" lets the model pick the safe tool with confidence.
- Say if it *runs now* or *runs on a schedule*. A recipe that sets a watch for
  one future event must say that it waits. It must say it is not a repeating
  schedule. That is what steers the model between running it and scheduling
  it.
- Name the inputs it needs. Then the model asks you for missing values
  instead of guessing.

The tool result is the recipe's `output.render`. Those are the same sections
the panel shows. Start with a summary. Mark `copyable` blocks: a drafted
reply, a generated snippet, the things you will paste somewhere else. Offer
the next step as a `button` action that points at the acting recipe. Do not
offer it as prose that the model would have to read and guess at.

If a run reaches a held approval, the result shows that it is waiting for
approval. It finishes later, when you decide, not because the model tries
again.

A run started from chat goes through the same gate as everything else. Reads
run under their grants. A write shows you an approval. You can fix the
details before you say yes. A burst of identical writes asks once for the
whole batch. You can relax the per-action ask for one session. You can relax
it for exactly this action, for a batch, or for a whole class of operation.
Only you can turn a repeated approval into a standing rule. See
[Grants and approvals](../concepts/grants-and-approvals.md).

Write the recipe with the ask in mind. The step that pauses should carry
enough labeled context that the approval reads as a real decision. Think
recipient, subject, and amount. And never split one real action into many
small operations to sneak under the approval. The audit diary shows it
anyway.

Chat can also set a schedule for an installed recipe. Each schedule carries
its own settings. Make your variables cover the things people will change per
schedule. Keep the description honest about what a run with nobody watching
does. The rules in [Triggers and watchers](authoring-triggers.md) apply just
the same.

All of this reaches past the built-in chat. The MCP door offers the same
exposed recipes as tools. Claude Desktop, Cursor, and any connected agent get
them, under that door's grants. See [AI chat and MCP](ai-chat-and-mcp.md)
and [Connect to Recued](connect-to-recued.md).

- Expose on purpose. Starting recipes and review recipes: on. Producers,
  reactive halves, and proposal-only actors: off.
- Arguments flat, labeled, with defaults. Prefer things people know over raw
  ids.
- Description: starts with a verb. Says what it reads, writes, and never
  does. Says run-now or schedule. Names the inputs.
- A call on defaults only works, or it stops cleanly.
- Results start with a summary. Next steps are buttons.
- Test the pick: ask chat to do the job with some look-alike tools around.
  Check that it picks your recipe and fills it in right.

Publishing puts a recipe or pack in the marketplace, under your name. A pack
is how you ship your own ingredients together with the recipes that use
them. Browsing and installing never need an account. Publishing needs a
free one, because your name needs an owner. What you publish is the JSON
itself, and anyone can read it. That openness is how the marketplace earns
trust.

Finish first. Test against your own server. For an ingredient pack, use the
Pack editor to save, review, preview, and install it on your server. Only
then open the cloud publish flow. The metadata makes the listing, so get it
right:

- **Name, description, tags.** How people find it.
- **Platforms and variant group.** Lets copies of one recipe for other
  platforms fold into one marketplace card.
- **Execution scope.** Badges that say where the recipe can run.
- **Provenance flag.** If you opt out of timeline links, people who install
  are shown that.
- **Fork lineage.** A published fork shows what it came from.

The publish screen takes one exported JSON object. It checks it and sends
it in. It is not an editor. Load a Kitchen handoff if your build offers one.
Or upload the exported file. Or paste the object. Then:

1. Confirm the artifact type is recipe.
2. Confirm the namespace. Your local slug becomes `publisher/slug`.
3. Checks run. They find schema errors. They apply the marketplace gates.
   They also warn about packs it needs that are missing. Each problem is
   listed by field.
4. Submit. The slug is saved for you while the review is pending.

What you sent in is pending until it is approved, rejected, or you cancel
it. Approval makes the live listing. A rejection shows its reason and its
time. Fix it in the Kitchen and send it again. The record is the status,
the reason, and the time. Nothing is hidden. Was it rejected or dropped?
Then its saved slug expires. Nobody can squat a name that way. Track all of
it on the dashboard's Submissions page.

Packs do not go through the recipe review queue. They use a separate,
direct path. The publisher you are signed in as must match the manifest's
`publisher`. Recued checks the pack envelope and every by-value
composition. A valid manifest is then published. It shows up in the
dashboard activity feed.

Direct publishing does not make a pack trusted. It does not make it a
first-party pack that is already installed for everyone. It does not prove
that every outside pin will resolve on the server of the person who
installs it. Installing still looks up the pinned versions. It still shows
the permission and connection choices. And it still stops safely on an
invalid composition. See the
[pack manifest reference](../reference/pack-manifest.md) for the two
manifest versions and what each one checks.

A new recipe version goes through review again. A new pack version goes
through the direct pack path and its checks again. Listings keep their
version history. People who install can stay pinned to a version instead of
following updates by themselves.

A fork is your own copy of someone's recipe. Forks are first-class. There
is a clear line between private and public:

- **Local forks** stay on your own setup. They are private. They run under
  the credential scope of the author of the original ingredient. That scope
  is the box that holds the secret keys.
- **Published forks** become their own thing. They get your publisher
  handle and your own credential scope. They show `fork_of`, which points
  back to the original.

Credential scope is per publisher and per install. So two recipes with the
same name from other publishers never share secrets.

Where the rules allow, you can take a listing down from the dashboard. You
can also put it back. Taking it down removes the listing from the
marketplace. It does not reach into servers that already installed the
content. Installs are local copies.

- [Account and dashboard](account-and-dashboard.md). Your handle, and where
  you track what you sent in.
- [Authoring recipes](authoring-recipes.md). Writing the thing you are
  about to publish.
- [Authoring ingredient packs](authoring-ingredient-packs.md). Building,
  reviewing, previewing, and installing your own capability on your server.
- [Recipes and packs](recipes-and-packs.md). How listings are browsed and
  installed.
- [Pack manifest](../reference/pack-manifest.md). The shape of a direct
  publish bundle, the packs it needs, and what it shows at install.

Reception is your server's safe front door. It is a set of public pages that
people outside can use. They can book a time, fill in a form, hand you a
file, or answer an approval. Your own server serves the pages. They never go
through Recued's cloud. A visitor needs nothing but the link.

- **Reception pages**: pages you build from blocks. A block can be text, a
  form, or links.
- **Scheduling links**: offer time slots and take bookings.
- **Intake forms**: a form with set fields. It collects a request from a
  client or someone you work with.
- **File drops**: a place where someone can hand you a file.
- **Approval links**: let one chosen person answer a question you sent to
  them.

section: Make a page from a template or a sentence
body:
There are two ways to make a page. Both give you the same kind of page. You
can pick a template from the gallery and fill in its slots. Or you can say
what you want in one sentence and let AI suggest the page. A template is
built from its slot values the same way every time. AI can make the words
better and guess at optional defaults. But AI is never needed. A server that
is offline, or has no model set up, can still publish every first-party
template. Either way, you look at the suggested page and fix it before it
goes live.

By default, Reception works like this: you review first, then you approve.
When someone sends something in, nothing runs. The request becomes a held
action. It waits at the same gate as everything else. It lands in your inbox.
There you can see what was sent. You can fix the details if they need it.
Then you approve or decline. Nothing a visitor sends runs before you decide.

A file a visitor sends lands in your warehouse, like any other file that
comes in. The warehouse is the place on your server that keeps your data. The
file stays attached to the request. You can add scanner packs. They can check
a file and add a note about it before you open it. The note is advice only.

A public page needs a public name. See
[Reachability](../setup/reachability.md). The name points straight at your
server. The page, the things people send, and the files never pass through
the cloud.

- [Grants and approvals](../concepts/grants-and-approvals.md): the gate that
  holds requests that come in.
- [Selling access](selling-access.md): a reception page can hold the link to
  a seller's checkout.

A recipe is a list of steps. It describes one job. A pack is a box you
install. The box can hold recipes, compositions, other packs it needs, and
the access those things need.

Each recipe stays visible on its own in the marketplace. That way you can see
what it does before you install anything. Some recipes belong to a pack.
When you install one of those, Recued finds the pack that owns it. Then it
opens that pack's setup screen.

This keeps two useful views:

1. **Recipe view.** What the recipe does, and what result it gives.
2. **Pack view.** What gets installed together, and which capabilities get
   access. A capability is one thing a pack can do.

A bulk pack may hold only recipes. That is still useful. The pack pins one set of
recipe versions that fit together. You review and install them in one go.
The pack page should show off those recipes. It should not show empty
sections about capabilities.

A recipe can need a capability pack. During setup, Recued shows you which
known packs are missing. You can install them first, together with the
recipe. Packs
you already have stay visible. They are not installed a second time.

Do you want the JSON for recipe pins, typed contents, and needed versions?
See the [pack manifest reference](../reference/pack-manifest.md).

A pack that uses a connection asks you two things:

- **Access.** Which operations the pack may use. For example, read only, or
  read and write.
- **Audience.** Who may use those grants. The default is only you, the owner.

The grant you pick attaches to the installed pack. A single recipe cannot
quietly make it bigger.

section: Risk and approval for an operation
body:
The access you pick at install time decides *which* operations a pack may
use. Two more fields on each operation decide how it acts when it runs:

- **`risk_tier`**. How serious its effect is: `read`, `write`, `admin`, or
  `destructive`. The
  [ingredient manifest reference](../reference/ingredient-manifest.md) says
  what each tier means.
- **`approval`**. When Recued stops and asks you before it runs: `never`,
  `ask`, or `always`.

The risk tier picks a sensible default. The `approval` field lets the author
change it. You write both on each operation. In a pack's composition rows,
they are the `risk` and `approval` fields. In the Kitchen ingredient builder,
they are the **Risk** and **Approval** dropdowns on each operation card.

Some operations matter but are not dangerous. They spend real money. They
start a costly render. They send something in your name. For these, you
usually want Recued to stop and ask **every time it runs**. Even when you are
the one pressing the button. The direct way to say that is to keep an honest
risk tier and set approval to always:

```json
{ "risk_tier": "admin", "approval": "always" }
```

`approval: "always"` means standing trust never waves this operation
through. It asks you on every run. You can still say yes for the current
chat session or for a burst. That way you are not clicking the same button
over and over. Turning it into a permanent rule that runs with nobody
watching is a separate, deliberate step. `admin` is a good base tier here. It reads as
"touches billing or spend". And it never quietly turns into a standing rule
on its own.

`destructive` also pauses every time. But it means something stronger. It
means an operation you **cannot take back**, like a delete or a bulk update.
It asks every time, *and you can never trust it away*. Its question says
"cannot be undone". Save it for things that really cannot be undone. Do not
use it just because something is costly.

So keep the two ideas apart. Use `approval: "always"` for an action that
costs money but *can* be undone, like a costly render. The owner can still
trust that away for one session. Save `destructive` for things that *cannot*
be undone. Then "cannot be undone" always means exactly that. What the owner
sees is covered in [Grants and approvals](../concepts/grants-and-approvals.md):
the approval card, session grants, and standing-rule suggestions.

A watcher is a recipe that keeps checking for something. Some watchers use
several packs that have nothing to do with each other. Such a watcher does
not need to pretend one pack owns them all. It can stay a recipe on its own.
You install it by hand. Each capability pack keeps its own install and its
own grants.

A seller runs things on their own server. That can be tools or automations.
It can be a knowledge base they look after. The seller sells or gives access to them
through an access type they open on purpose: MCP tools, MCP chat, or an
OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Customers connect from any MCP client or any
OpenAI-compatible chat client. They do not need Recued. Money moves on your own payment system. Recued takes no cut. It handles
no payment. It carries none of the traffic. Zero percent, forever.

You sell access in **tiers**. A tier can be `basic`, `pro`, or whatever
fits your product. Each tier is backed by a **customer contract template**. That is a
normal contract you write in your contracts screen. A contract is the saved
list of what one actor may do. The template holds just the tools and
scopes that tier grants. It also holds the usage policy. That says how much a
customer may use per period. It also says how many calls per minute are
allowed. Usage is counted in tool calls and chat turns. It is never counted
in model tokens.

A template is a hard ceiling. Automation can open, extend, and close customer
access stamped *from* a template. But nothing can widen a grant past what you
wrote. Not a payment webhook (a message another service sends to your server
when something happens). Not a recipe. Not even a hacked provider
account. What is the worst a fake subscription event can do? It can give the
access a paying customer would have gotten.

The money is yours to handle, in either mode:

- **Manual**: an invoice, a free pass, a trial, another store. You open and
  close access yourself. Recued writes down when access opens and closes,
  not the payment.
- **Provider-automated**: a payment provider drives the whole flow. Stripe,
  Paddle, and Lemon Squeezy are supported. Subscription events work by
  themselves. They open, extend, swap tiers, and close access against your
  tiers. You do not
  wire up the event handling yourself. It installs as one pack. See
  [Turning on provider automation](#turning-on-provider-automation).

Checkout is hosted by the provider. Card details never come near your server.
Your public [reception page](reception.md) shows a link to the checkout and
nothing more. You are the merchant of record. That means the business the
customer buys from, in the eyes of the law. Taxes, refunds, and invoices
live with you and your provider. Recued does not send invoices. It does not
hold money. It does not work out part-period charges. It keeps no money
ledger. It opens and closes access.

1. A subscription starts, or you give access by hand. A customer access row
   is stamped from the tier's template.
2. The customer gets a **claim link** by mail. The mail never carries the raw
   token.
   The claim page shows the token once. Next to it are the addresses to
   connect to.
   There are also copy-and-paste settings to use. They cover Claude Desktop,
   Cursor, a plain MCP client, and an OpenAI-compatible client.
3. A renewal extends access. A plan change swaps the tier. A failed payment
   opens a grace window that you control. It is 72 hours by default. So a
   customer is not cut off at the first retry. A cancellation, a refund, or a
   dispute closes access right away. Each of those defaults is set per
   status. You can change them.
4. If a token leaks, you issue a new one. The new one kills the old one. The
   customer gets a fresh claim link.

One-time purchases work as **time-boxed passes**. A pass lasts a fixed time.
Its usage policy caps how much can be used in total.

A customer token is just one more actor with a contract. It stands at the
same gate as everything else. It reaches just the tools its tier grants.
It has its own rate and period limits. Every call is marked with its name and written in the
audit diary. Three access types cover the common product shapes:

- **MCP tools**: the tools you granted show up in the customer's own agent.
- **Peer chat**: another Recued asks your server's AI over the MCP link.
- **OpenAI-compatible endpoint**: a base URL plus an API key for chat apps.
  Use it when the product is "ask my operated knowledge". Do not use it for
  "call my tools from your agent."

Self-service goes through the same access. A status operation returns the
customer's own usage, limits, and tier. It also says when the period ends.
So "how much
have I used?" is a question their own AI can answer. You do not run an
extra customer website.

Every provider works the same way. Two packs, installed once from the
marketplace:

- **The seller catalog**: *Stripe for Sellers*, *Paddle for Sellers*, or
  *Lemon Squeezy for Sellers*. Only the operations that selling really needs.
  On purpose, this is not the provider's whole API. Granting it does not hand
  your automations the rest of your account.
- **The events pack**: the whole billing lifecycle in one install. Its
  handlers sit behind one webhook binding. They cover checkout done, renewal,
  failed payment, and plan change. They also cover cancelling. Pause and
  resume are covered where the provider has them. So you pick one delivery endpoint and
  the flow works.
  You do not build it event by event.

Then add the connection. Point the provider's webhook at the endpoint the
pack asks for. The pack also asks for a **category**. It is the group your
tiers and their customers belong to. Keep the default unless you sell separate
products whose tier keys would clash. Open Settings → Seller → Setup →
Providers and run **Synchronize tiers**. It makes one tier per Stripe
entitlement feature. On Paddle or Lemon Squeezy it makes one per product. An
entitlement feature is what a paid plan says the customer gets.
You write each tier's grants in the contracts screen. That step is yours by
design. Nothing else can do it for you.

section: Before you install the provider pack
body:
Two things to know first:

- **The install signs that endpoint up for all seven event types.** They are
  parts of one flow. They are not a menu. So you choose the pack, not the
  event.
  What each handler *does* stays yours. The per-status policy above decides
  what a failed payment means. It can mean a grace window, an instant close,
  or nothing at all.
- **The events only remove the wait.** A regular check reads your provider
  straight. It lines up customer state on its own timer. So a server that was
  offline when an event was sent still catches up. A webhook you never got
  cannot quietly leave a customer stuck. The events just make it all react
  in seconds. Without them it waits for the next check.

Refunds and disputes are the one place where you choose instead of install.
**Revoke Access** cuts a customer off when a charge is fully refunded or
disputed. **Flag for Review** only raises a notice. It does that even on
partial refunds. So you can judge case by case. They ship as two packs. A
seller wants one or the other, never both.

section: Selling through Paddle or Lemon Squeezy
body:
Each provider is a self-contained lane from checkout to close. Its own
seller catalog and events pack. Its own webhook endpoint and tiers. Adding one never touches another. Lemon Squeezy has no automatic
webhook setup. You paste the endpoint into its dashboard yourself.

With Paddle and Lemon Squeezy, tiers come from your products. A subscription
always says which product it is for. So renewals, plan changes, and the
normal check all line up against that product id. Lemon Squeezy asks for
your store id as well. Its product list is per store.

Both providers are the merchant of record. That means they add tax on top
of your price and pay you out. So Recued compares your offer amount with
the price before tax. Set the offer amount to the product's price and the
numbers match.

One-time passes work on both providers too, and need no product at all. A
pass is a tier you create by hand, with a duration. The offer names it. On
Paddle, the checkout carries the pass as an inline item. The item has the
offer's price and name. You also pick a tax category for each offer. Nothing
is saved
to your Paddle catalog. On Lemon Squeezy, a checkout always needs a variant.
So you create one single-payment variant once, at any price. Every pass
checkout then pins the offer's price and name on it, for that checkout only.
The
buyer pays, the pass pack confirms the payment, and the claim link goes out
by mail. Each pass pack asks for its own webhook endpoint. That holds on
Stripe too. The pass pack watches for its own paid sessions, apart from the
subscription events pack.

section: What differs with Paddle and Lemon Squeezy
body:
Some differences you will see:

- Paddle pauses and resumes subscriptions. A pause opens the grace window
  you set for it. A resume extends access again on the same customer row.
- A Lemon Squeezy cancellation keeps access until the paid period ends. Only
  the expiry closes it.
- Lemon Squeezy cannot read a checkout's custom data back. The order key
  rides only in its signed webhook. So each handler checks the tie a second
  way. The subscription's order must be the order your server recorded.
- There is no Lemon Squeezy missed-grant sweep. Its API does not say which
  subscriptions your server sold. The regular check still lines up every
  customer it already knows.

Neither pack has been driven against a live provider account yet. The
handlers were built from the provider docs. Try them in the provider's test
mode first.

Settings → Seller is where you run things. Each area is its own screen:
overview, offers, orders, tiers, customers, usage, and setup. Every screen,
every record, and every setup step has its own address. So you can bookmark
a tier, or link a customer straight to their order. The grants themselves are
always written by you in the contracts screen. Some practical rules:

- Sell from a server that is always on and reachable. A small VPS (a rented
  server that stays on), not a home
  IP. `<handle>.recued.net` is the starter name. Serious sellers move on to a
  custom domain on their own DNS.
- Test your provider's test mode from start to finish before you go live.
- Your uptime is your customers' uptime.
- Prefer prepaid flat tiers. Or a base fee with extra charges past a limit.
  Or time-boxed passes. Pure pay-after-use billing means you deliver first and
  collect later. The invoice comes at the end of the period. If it fails, you
  cannot take back what was already used.

section: What this changes for everyone else
body:
Nothing. If you never sell, contracts, outside access, and approvals work
just as before. Customer rows never show up among your normal contracts. The
marketplace stays free to browse, install, and publish. Selling access is
something your server can do. It is not a marketplace fee.

- [Grants and approvals](../concepts/grants-and-approvals.md): the gate that
  customer calls pass through.
- [AI chat and MCP](ai-chat-and-mcp.md): the access types customers connect
  through.
- [Reachability](../setup/reachability.md): giving your server a steady
  public name.

Recued sits between an AI and your accounts. The AI can read useful things
through Recued. It can do useful things through Recued. But the AI never gets
your secret keys. And the cloud never becomes the owner of your data.

> **Local first.** Your server runs everything. It is in charge of who you
> are. It keeps the diary of what happened. It is the only part of Recued
> that talks to your accounts.

- [Set up Recued](getting-started.md) and pair your first device.
- See [how the four parts of Recued fit together](concepts/how-recued-works.md).
- See [what stays on your server and what can leave](concepts/security-and-privacy.md).
- Learn why [you browse recipes one by one, but install packs as one box](guides/recipes-and-packs.md).

| Area | What you will find |
| --- | --- |
| Setup | How to install, pair, get reached from outside, update, back up, and set up AI |
| Concepts | Safety, privacy, who you are, grants, approvals, the audit diary, and what stays local |
| Guides | Connections, recipes, packs, writing your own, publishing, and selling access |
| Reference | The exact fields for recipes, ingredients, and packs, the transforms, and the glossary |

This site explains what the product does and supports. The deeper design
papers and decision records live next to the source code. So do the notes
for people who help build Recued.

A pack is a box that holds recipes and ingredients. A **composition** is the
capability half of that box. It names one surface Recued can talk
to. And it lists the operations a recipe may call on that surface.

The [Pack editor](../guides/authoring-ingredient-packs.md) makes a
composition for you. Most authors never read this page. It is here for two
reasons. You may want to generate a pack with a tool instead of typing it.
The tool could read an API description. It could be a script. It could be a
program of your own. Publishing a pack you did not write by hand is a
supported path.

Everything below is exactly what publish and install check.

```json
{
  "manifest_version": 2,
  "artifact_type": "pack",
  "pack_kind": "app_pack",
  "slug": "acme-tasks",
  "publisher": "your-publisher-handle",
  "name": "Acme Tasks",
  "description": "Read and act on Acme tasks.",
  "version": 1,
  "recipes": [],
  "tags": ["pack:acme"],
  "contents": [{ "type": "composition", "composition": { } }]
}
```

`publisher` must be the handle you are signed in as when you publish. The
[pack manifest](pack-manifest.md) page explains the rest of the outer part
(the envelope).

```json
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "slug": "acme-catalog",
  "catalog_kind": "official",
  "ingredients": [],
  "operations": []
}
```

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `schema_version` | `1` |
| `slug` | Required. The name of the catalog |
| `catalog_kind` | `official`, `unofficial_acknowledged`, or `private_byo`. This says how official your description of the vendor is |
| `ingredients` | **Exactly one row.** See below |
| `operations` | **At least one row** |

One composition describes one surface. So `ingredients` has one entry only.
Does a vendor have two API versions that do not work together? Then make two
packs. The second pack depends on the first one. It does not add a second
ingredient.

section: Ingredients — what you can talk to
body:
```json
{
  "slug": "acme-catalog",
  "kind": "http",
  "http": {
    "base": "https://api.acme.example",
    "connection": "acme",
    "result_path": "items"
  },
  "entities": {}
}
```

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `slug` | Each operation's `ingredient` field points at this |
| `kind` | `http`, `cli`, `connection`, `mcp`, or `storage` |
| `http.base` | **Origin only.** Put the full path in each operation's `path_template` |
| `http.connection` | Which connection record holds the secret keys |
| `http.result_path` | The default place where records sit in a response. An operation may set its own |
| `entities` | You can skip it. Vendor entity schemas, for a pack that maps records into a standard shape |

⚠ **Keep `base` origin-only.** Say the base ends with a version prefix. And
say an operation path starts with `/`. Then the prefix gets dropped. That is
just how web addresses join together. Both forms work today. But origin-only
is the rule everyone follows. It never surprises anyone.

A `kind: "storage"` ingredient is different. It is a pack with its own rows
on your server, not a remote API. See
[Authoring ingredient packs](../guides/authoring-ingredient-packs.md) for what
that can and cannot do.

section: Operations — what a recipe can call

body:
| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `op` | The name a recipe calls. Once installed it is `publisher.pack.op` |
| `ingredient` | The ingredient slug above |
| `risk` | `read`, `write`, `admin`, or `destructive` |
| `approval` | `never`, `ask`, or `always` |
| `idempotency` | `safe`, `idempotent`, or `non_idempotent` |
| `description` | What an AI model reads to decide whether to pick this |
| `args` | The inputs a caller can pass. See below |
| `bind` | How the call is made. See below |
| `result_path` | Where records sit in this operation's response. **This beats the surface default** |
| `pagination` | You can skip it. Says how paging works |
| `cache_ttl_ms` | You can skip it. How long to keep a cached response |

🔑 **`risk` and `approval` are the real safety controls.** What an operation
may do is decided by two things. One is the grant it runs under. The other is
the approval gate. It is never decided by how well the vendor is documented.
It is never decided by how the operation is named. Declare what the operation really
does. An operation that changes someone else's data is not `read`. That is
true even if it happens to be a `GET`.

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `key` | The name a recipe uses to pass it. A dotted start says where it goes: `query.*`, `body.*`, or `header.*`. A bare name is a path variable |
| `type` | `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `object`, `array` |
| `required` | True means the call cannot run without it |
| `affects_target` | Marks the argument that says **which** record is touched. The approval gate uses it to explain how much could change |

The name of a path variable is **yours** to choose. It is not the vendor's
name. It is the `{{task_id}}` in your own `path_template`. It is not the name
in the vendor's API description.

| `bind.kind` | Carries |
| --- | --- |
| `rest` | `method`, `path_template`, optional `static_query`, `static_headers`, `static_body` |
| `graphql` | The query text and the variable mapping |
| `cli_invocation` | A list of arguments for a local command. Never one shell string with values pasted in |
| `core.records` | An `action` and an `entity` on the pack's own local rows |

⭐ **`static_query` is how you ask for fields.** Some vendors only return the
fields you ask for. If yours does, every field your pack reads later must be
asked for here. Otherwise that field comes back empty at run time. It fails
quietly. You will think "the vendor sent nothing." The truth is "I never
asked."

Some APIs return whole numbers too big for JavaScript to hold exactly. For
those, declare `bind.response_json: { "unsafe_integers": "string" }`. Then an
id is never rounded by mistake. Big numbers arrive as exact text. Everything
else keeps its normal JSON type.

section: How long a local command may run
body:
Every `cli_invocation` op is **awaited**. Recued starts it, waits for it to
finish, and gets its real result. There is no "start it and hand back a
receipt" mode for normal work. The `timeout_ms` setting says how long that
wait may last. It has three states:

| `timeout_ms` | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| omitted | the catalog's normal deadline |
| a positive number | a hard time limit of that many milliseconds |
| **`0`** | **unbounded: no time limit at all** |

⭐ **`0` is not a trick. It is the honest choice for work whose length you
truly cannot guess.** A transcode (turning a media file into another
format), an AI agent task, or a large download. Authors used to write a
progress declaration that declared no progress at all. That removed the
deadline as a side effect. That spelling is gone. Say `0` and mean it.

`progress` tells Recued how to see that a command is still working. A stuck
command gets killed. A slow but working one is left alone.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `contract` | `heartbeat` (the tool prints progress) or `file-growth` (an output file gets bigger) |
| `adapter` | **heartbeat only.** Names the code on the host that can read this tool's progress |
| `watch_path` | **file-growth only.** The file to watch |
| `stall_ms` | How long with no progress before the run is killed. **Required** |

⛔ **`adapter` is a fixed list, not any text you like.** A heartbeat needs
code that understands the tool's output. You cannot turn random output into
progress just by naming it. Does your tool have no adapter? Use `file-growth`
if it writes its output bit by bit. Or use a fixed `timeout_ms`.

⚠ `stall_ms` must be **less than** a positive `timeout_ms`. A stall limit
longer than the deadline can never fire. With `timeout_ms: 0` there is no
deadline at all. Then `stall_ms` is the only limit.

`detached` is for **services**. A service is a program that stays running,
like a tunnel or a local AI model server. Using `detached` is not a way to
make a normal command return early.

Every detached op must declare `supervision`. And supervision must declare
readiness:

```json
{
  "kind": "cli_invocation",
  "argv_template": ["mytool", "serve"],
  "stdin_handling": "none",
  "shape": "text",
  "exit_code_handling": "zero_is_success",
  "detached": {
    "mode": "runtime_managed",
    "completion": { "kind": "marker_file", "exit_pattern": "{dir}/{key}.exit.{code}" },
    "cancel": { "kind": "process_group", "pid_pattern": "{dir}/{key}.pid" },
    "supervision": {
      "restart_policy": "on-crash",
      "readiness": { "kind": "http_ok", "url": "http://127.0.0.1:9099/ready" },
      "ready_timeout_ms": 30000
    }
  }
}
```

⛔ **A running process does not mean ready.** A freshly started service can
crash seconds later. So "the pid exists" is a *wrong* answer, not just a weak
one. Readiness kinds are a fixed list. It is the same list the service
checkers use: `http_ok`, `tcp_open`, `pid_file`, `file_exists`, `exec_ok`,
`binary_in_path`. Publishing supervision without one is refused.

⚠ A detached op cannot declare `output_capture` or `input_materialize`. A
service reports that it is ready. It does not return a file.

A command that makes a big file returns a **reference**, not the bytes.
Declare `output_capture`. Then the file is streamed into the user's file
store. The recipe and the AI model both get a handle to it. The webclient
shows it as a link, or as a picture when it is an image. Nothing big ever
goes through the value channel. So there is no size limit for you to
declare.

An ingredient names a `connection`. A connection is a saved way to talk to an
outside service. That record holds the secret key, **locked with strong (AEAD)
encryption on the user's own server**. The key is never in your pack. It is
never in Recued's cloud. It is never in the manifest you publish.

- **Using a vendor Recued already knows:** name it by slug. At install, the
  user picks one of their existing connections.
- **Bringing a new vendor:** the user adds it through the general connection
  form. That form asks for a base URL and the auth details. Recued's setup
  guide fills the gap. It points at the vendor's developer page. It works out
  the auth type. It suggests values for each field. So an author who brings
  an unknown vendor does not hand users a blank form.

You know your vendor's base URL. You know where its tokens come from. Say so.
Then the form opens with those boxes already filled in:

```json
{
  "connection_hints": [
    {
      "connection": "acme",
      "values": {
        "config.base_url": "https://api.acme.example",
        "auth.scope": "tasks.read tasks.write"
      },
      "setup_url": "https://acme.example/developers/tokens"
    }
  ]
}
```

`connection_hints` sits next to `contents` in the manifest. **Every
publisher** may use it. `connection` names a connection that one of your
ingredients uses.

A hint sets a **value**. It can only set a field the user can see and edit.
It cannot hide a field. It cannot lock one. It cannot show a hidden one. Those
powers belong to the connection form, not to your pack. So if you get a value
wrong, the user sees it and fixes it. It never happens to them behind their
back. A pre-filled box shows your publisher handle as a label, until the user
edits it.

| Field key | Pre-fills |
| --- | --- |
| `config.base_url` | The API address |
| `subresource_path` | The sub-resource permission boundary |
| `auth.scope`, `auth.scopes` | The scopes you ask for |
| `auth.token_endpoint`, `auth.authorize_url` | The OAuth addresses |
| `auth.param_name` | The query-parameter name for key auth |

**A key on that list can still do nothing, quietly.** Publishing only checks
that the key is spelled right. It does not check that your connection's form
really shows that field. A hint is dropped in two cases. One: the form has no
such field. Two: the form pins the field. (A registered vendor may fix its
own endpoint. A hint may not move it.) The OAuth keys only appear after the
user picks a matching OAuth auth type. Those keys are `auth.scope`,
`auth.scopes`, `auth.token_endpoint`, and `auth.authorize_url`. So hinting
them does nothing for a user who signs in with an API key. Nothing warns you
about any of this, at publish or at install. Hint only the keys your
connection really uses. Then check the form once with a real install.

section: What a hint may not do
body:
Nothing else is accepted. A key that is not on that list **fails your
publish**. It is not quietly dropped. An endpoint value must be a public
`https` URL with no secret in it. These are refused: `http`, `localhost`, a
private address, and a `user:password@` prefix. A value over 500 characters
is refused too. `setup_url` follows the same rules. It is a link you are
asking someone to click.

There is no secret key here, and there cannot be one. A hint fills in the
boxes around a secret. The secret itself always comes from the user.

A pack may have at most **eight** hint entries. An entry has `connection`,
`values`, and `setup_url`, and nothing else. The `connection_requirements`
fields (`api_base`, `vendor`, `authority`, `identity_endpoint`, `auth`,
`per_org`) are refused inside a hint. They are not ignored. So a line you
thought was accepted never quietly does nothing.

The pre-fill shows up *after* your pack is installed. It is not on the
install screen. The path is: install → the pack's **Connections** row →
**Set up →** → the form, filled in and labelled with your handle. The install
screen names the connection your pack wants. So the user knows that before
they grant anything. But the install screen does not open the form. Nothing
is installed yet at that point. So there is no pack to read hints from. Write
your setup instructions in that order.

**You can** write a full composition. You can bring a vendor Recued has never
heard of. You can ship with no API description at all. You can declare
synced Sources. You can pre-fill the connection form with
`connection_hints`. And you can publish and install. This whole path is
tested end to end.

**You cannot** declare `connection_requirements`. That field is not a bigger
hint. It decides which of the user's *existing* connections your pack is
offered for. It tags a connection as a certain vendor. It names an OAuth
issuer. It gives the endpoint used to spot duplicate accounts. Each of those
things acts without the user reading a form. That is why only Recued's own
publisher may use it, wired into first-party setup code.

In practice the difference is one click. A first-party pack can show
**Connect account** on the install screen. Your pack asks the user to add the
connection through the form. With hints and the setup guide, that form
arrives mostly filled in. But it is still a form. It is honest to say so,
not to pretend they are the same.

**You cannot** write `trust_summary`. Recued works out verification itself.
A publisher cannot claim it. A self-published pack cannot mark itself
verified. That is the whole point.

⏭ These two things are linked. The direction matters while you build. One
day, publisher verification should be what earns a smoother way to add a
connection (the one-click **Connect account**). That flow should not stay
first-party forever. That work is not built yet.
This page will change when it is.

section: What publishing checks, and what it does not
body:
| | Publish | Install |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The shape of the composition: a missing table, an unknown `kind`, an operation that names no ingredient | rejected | rejected |
| An API description the catalog does not pin | rejected | rejected |
| Shipping no API description at all | fine | fine |
| A field path that names something the API never returns | **not checked** | **not checked** |

That last row is on purpose. It is worth understanding. No machine checks a
field path. Testing an operation proves its method and its route. It proves
nothing about the fields inside a response. A check built on that would pass
while proving nothing that matters. Then "it passed" would sound like "it was
verified" to a reader. A check that looks like proof but is not one is worse
than no check at all.

Instead, Recued makes the problem visible. The runtime reports any declared
field that has never held a value on any record. That is exactly what a wrong
path looks like. First-party and third-party packs are treated the same way.

⇒ **Your own declaration is the control, not the gate.** Test your paths
against the operation as you shipped it. Do not test against a hand-made
request that happens to work.

**A field that is never filled may be a wrong path. Or it may be your own
filter.** Before you blame the declaration, re-read the list operation that
feeds it. Say a field only exists on closed records. And say your query
leaves out closed records. Then that field can never be filled. The path was
right. The scope was wrong.

**A list that returns only ids must be filled out with reads.** Say the list
gives back only `{ id, url }`. And say every real field arrives only when you
read one record. Then measuring the list alone reports every field as never
seen. That is a shape effect, not a broken declaration.

- [Authoring ingredient packs](../guides/authoring-ingredient-packs.md): the
  editor path, and the one to start with.
- [Pack manifest](pack-manifest.md): the envelope this sits inside.
- [Publishing](../guides/publishing.md): submission, validation, review.
- [Recipe schema](recipe-schema.md): what calls these operations.
Each word gets a short meaning. Where a page says more, there is a link.

**Actor** — who an action runs as. That can be you. It can be one of your
automations. It can be an outside party with a contract, such as a connected
AI agent or a customer. Every audit entry names its actor.

**Approval** — an action that is paused and waits for your decision. It
keeps waiting until you answer. Often you can change its details first. See
[Grants and approvals](../concepts/grants-and-approvals.md).

**Archive** — one encrypted file that ends in `.recued.archive`. It holds a
full backup of your server. See
[Backup and restore](../setup/backup-and-restore.md).

**Audit** — the diary. Every run writes a record on your server. It says who
asked (the actor), on which channel, what was read, what was written, and
how it ended. See [Audit and memory](../concepts/audit-and-memory.md).

**Batch mode** — one AI call that runs a contracted AI function on every item
in a list. You turn it on with `llm.id_field`.

**Browser Bridge** — a small add-on for your web browser. It watches for the
page triggers a recipe declared. It reads web pages and does things on them,
like clicking or typing. It
shows notifications from your computer's own system. It does all of this
only for your server. It runs only signed commands from the server. It holds
no data.

**BYOK** — bring your own key. These are your paid or self-hosted AI models.
They go in the two slots for normal AI. See [Set up AI](../setup/ai-setup.md).

**Category** — a seller's own label that groups access tiers with their
customers. Every server starts with one, called `main`, and most sellers
never change it. A second category is only for selling separate products
whose tier keys would clash. A category cannot change once a tier exists.

**Circuit breaker** — a safety switch. When a reactive recipe fails many
times in a row, the switch turns it off and tells you. You turn it back on
yourself.

**Claim link** — a link sent to a customer by mail. It does one job. The
customer follows it to pick up their access token. The token itself is never
sent by mail. See [Selling access](../guides/selling-access.md).

**Connection** — a saved way to talk to an outside service. It has a name,
and you can use it again and again. The service can be an API, an MCP
server, or a place to send notifications. The secret keys stay on your
server. See [Connections](../guides/connections.md).

**Contract** — the saved list of what someone may do. The gate that checks
every action reads it. It can cover an installed capability, a chat session,
or a customer tier.

**Customer** — an outside person or company that a seller gives access to,
at a chosen tier. A customer connects with any MCP client or any
OpenAI-compatible chat client. They do not need Recued.

**Door** — a way in from outside that you open on purpose. There are MCP
doors, reception doors, and messenger doors. Each door has its own grants,
tool by tool, and its own secret key.

**Enforcement boundary** — the one gate every action goes through. The gate
works out who is asking and which capability they use. It checks the grant
and the risk tier. It runs the action on your server. Then it writes the
audit record.

**Embeddings slot** — the one AI provider and model used for work that makes
vectors. Some recipes and some housekeeping need that. Chat never uses it.
Normal AI never uses it. If it is missing, nothing falls back to the free
pool or the BYOK slots.

**Enrichment** — a fact Recued works out ahead of time and sticks onto a
warehouse record. A score or a signal, for example. Some come from plain
math. Some come from AI, under the trust level you set for each topic.

**Free pool** — your own free-tier AI keys. Recued tries these before your
paid keys.

**Grant** — a yes you give ahead of time. It says which actions a pack, a
door, or a session may use. It says at what access level. And it says who
may use them.

**Housekeeping** — clean-up work the server does while the server is not
busy. It
packs the database, clears old cache, refreshes enrichments, and checks CRM
data against the vendor.

**Ingredient** — one action a recipe can use. A small file (a manifest)
describes it. It can be an HTTP call, a page action, an AI function, a
storage call, or a connection call. The file says what goes in, what comes
out, and how risky it is. See [Ingredient manifest](ingredient-manifest.md).

**Kitchen** — the place where you make, copy (fork), and test recipes and
ingredients before you publish them.

**LLM gateway** — your server's chat endpoint that speaks the OpenAI shape.
It answers at `/v1/models` and `/v1/chat/completions`. Any chat app that
takes a base URL and an API key can use it. Each turn follows the rules of
the contract it was granted. See
[Connect to Recued](../guides/connect-to-recued.md).

**Marketplace** — the public store of recipes, ingredients, and packs.
Looking and installing are free. Publishing needs a free account.

**MCP** — an open, shared language that outside AI apps use to call your
server's tools. See [AI chat and MCP](../guides/ai-chat-and-mcp.md).

**Memory** — your own notes: facts, choices, and things you let an AI save.
You own it. Nothing prunes it. Recall searches it. It is not the audit
diary. See [Audit and memory](../concepts/audit-and-memory.md).

**Pack** — a box that holds recipes, ingredients, and rules. You install the
whole box at once. Grants attach to the pack. See
[Recipes, ingredients, and packs](../concepts/recipes-ingredients-packs.md).

**Pairing** — linking a device (the webclient or the Bridge) to your server.
The device gets a limited pass. You can cancel it.
Pairing goes
straight to your server, never through the cloud.

**Pro** — a paid extra, $5.99 USD a month, and you can skip it. It gives your
server a `<handle>.recued.net` name and a certificate that renews by itself.
It unlocks no features.

**Publisher handle** — your name in the marketplace. It is free. Everything
you publish lives under it.

**Reception** — your server's public front door. It can show pages, forms,
booking links, and file drops. Every request that comes in waits for you to
review it. See [Reception](../guides/reception.md).

**Recipe** — a list of steps written in JSON that you can read. The steps
use ingredients and transforms to do one job. See
[Authoring recipes](../guides/authoring-recipes.md).

**Recovery key** — 24 secret words. They let a device pair. They unlock the
data your server encrypts. They also open your backup archives.

**Server** — the Recued program you run on a machine you control. It does
all the real work. It is the one part everything else trusts. It holds the
warehouse and your
secret keys. It runs the timers. It owns the audit diary. It is the only
part that touches your accounts.

**Tier** — a named level of access a seller offers. Behind each tier is a
customer contract template. That template fixes what the tier grants and how
much it may be used.

**Timeline** — one feed, in time order, for one thing, such as a person or a
deal. It is built
from provenance links across mail, calendar, CRM, notes (annotations), and
memory.

**Transform** — a small safe tool a recipe uses to work on data. It always
gives the same answer for the same input. It costs nothing. See
[Transforms](transforms.md).

**Trigger** — the web page patterns (URLs) a recipe is made for, so it can
auto-run there. This is not the same as `trigger_steps`. Those are the check
steps a reactive recipe runs to decide whether to go ahead.

**Warehouse** — the place on your server that keeps a copy of your mail,
calendar, contacts, files, and CRM records. Recipes and AI answers are based
on it. See [The warehouse](../concepts/warehouse.md).

**Watcher** — the trigger part of a reactive recipe. It watches mail, files,
the calendar, the clock, or web pages. Each tick, it decides whether the
recipe should go ahead.

**Webclient** — the app in your web browser at `app.recued.com`. Your own
server can serve it too. It shows things and takes your clicks and typing.
It does no
real work and holds no secret keys.

An ingredient is one operation a recipe can use. An operation is one thing
it can do, like a read or a call. It is written as a small file called a
manifest. The manifest says what goes in, what comes out, and how risky the
operation is. Recued checks the manifest when you install it or submit
it. The one gate every action goes through reads the manifest too. Nothing is
guessed while a recipe runs.

Here is an ingredient that reads one deal from HubSpot:

```json
{
  "slug": "deal-reader-hubspot",
  "author": "recued-core",
  "kind": "http",
  "category": "data",
  "risk_tier": "read",
  "input": {
    "method": "GET",
    "url": "{{vault.hubspot.base_url}}/crm/v3/objects/deals/{{deal_id}}",
    "header.authorization": "Bearer {{vault.hubspot.token}}",
    "deal_id": null,
    "query.properties": "dealname,amount,dealstage,closedate"
  },
  "output": {
    "deal_id": "response.id",
    "deal_name": "response.properties.dealname",
    "amount": "response.properties.amount"
  }
}
```

Each input key maps a target to a value. The value can be a plain value, a
`{{ref}}`, or `null`. A `null` means the caller must give the value. If a
`null` is never filled in, that is an error at install time. It is not a
surprise at run time. A key with no known prefix (like `deal_id`) is one of
the ingredient's own parameters. Other values can point to it as
`{{deal_id}}`.

The `kind` field is required. It names the adapter that runs the ingredient.
An adapter is the part of Recued that does one kind of work. The Kitchen
editor offers these adapters. Recued checks each one at install:

| `kind` | Executes | Where it runs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `http` | An HTTP or REST call to the outside | Server |
| `dom` | A page trigger, read, or write on a live website | The Browser Bridge, told what to do by the server |
| `ai` | A call to an AI model, or an embeddings call | Server |
| `mcp` | An MCP tool call | Server |
| `service` | A long-running service that was set up on the server | Server |
| `storage` | The warehouse, shared records, enrichments, and files | Server |
| `connection` | A call through a named connection | Server |

Each kind has rules about which input keys it must have and must not have.
An `http` manifest must declare `url`. An `ai` manifest must have at least
one `llm.*` key, and it may not have `url`. And so on. A manifest with the
wrong kind fails when you submit it. It never fails at run time. The `url`
string does a second job. It is a promise the validator holds you to. At
publish time, the validator pulls out its pattern. At run time, the real URL
must match that pattern.

The `category` field says what the operation is. A `data` operation reads. An
`ai` operation runs a model. An `action` operation changes something outside.
The `risk_tier` field says how Recued guards it:

| Tier | Governance |
| --- | --- |
| `read` | Runs quietly once it is granted |
| `write` | Needs your approval |
| `admin` | Needs your approval, plus a scope (which things it may touch) |
| `destructive` | Needs your approval, plus a clear extra yes |

Some operations are big but can be undone. They spend money, or they start a
costly render. Want Recued to ask every single time? Keep the tier at `write`
or `admin`, and set the catalog operation's `approval` to `always`. The owner
can still say yes for a whole session. Each kind allows only the tiers that
make sense. An `ai` manifest can only be `read`. Running a model cannot
destroy anything by itself. A destructive tool call belongs to `mcp` or
`connection`. A `dom` manifest stops at `write`. A tier that does not fit its
kind is rejected when you submit.

A `kind: 'connection'` ingredient calls through a named connection. It never
touches the secret key. The connection executor adds the key at call time.
The key is never written into the manifest:

| `connection_kind` | Required input | Shape |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `api` | `connection`, `method`, `path` | plus `query.*`, `header.*` (never auth), `body.*`, `body_raw` |
| `mcp` | `connection`, `tool` | plus `args` |
| `notification` | `connection`, `text` | plus `title`, `link_url`, and a `recipient` whose shape depends on the subtype |

The `connection` field always holds a `{{config.<name>}}` picker. At install,
the dialog asks the user to pick a connection that fits. A picker left empty
fails with a named error. It never guesses. A connection wrapper can also
carry `vault_hints`. That doubles as the set-up form for a new connection, shown
when no fitting connection exists yet. Every wrapper declares `permission` and `risk_tier`.
The gate runs before the adapter. The adapter only moves data in and out.

**HTTP and connection ingredients** map neat field names to paths in the
response. So the recipe sees `step.<id>.deal_name`, not the raw reply. An
entry can also be `["parse_number", "response.properties.amount"]`. That
applies a transform while the value is pulled out.

**DOM ingredients** flip the mapping. The key is a CSS selector (a pattern
that picks one part of the page) or a URL pattern. The value is the field name. The special value `trigger` marks the
URL pattern the page must match. A DOM ingredient in the `data` category
reads from the page. One in the `action` category writes input values into
the page.

The contracted `ai-*` functions have no platform at the end of their name.
AI does not belong to one platform. Their inputs, outputs, batch mode, and
model hints are in the [recipe schema](recipe-schema.md). Pick in this order.
First, try a transform. It always gives the same answer, and it is free.
Second, try a contracted AI function. Third, use `ai-prompt`. That last one
is the escape hatch with no fixed shape.

An `ai` manifest whose output declares `vector` is an embeddings ingredient.
It goes only to the dedicated Embeddings slot. It never goes to the free pool
or to the fast and quality BYOK slots (your own paid keys). Use that shape
only for work that truly needs vectors (lists of numbers that stand for
meaning). It is not another road for normal
AI.

A vault reference in a manifest belongs to its publisher. For example,
`{{vault.hubspot.token}}` is looked up under the ingredient author's own name
space. One publisher can never read another publisher's vault. Recued blocks
that at run time. A recipe never uses `{{vault.*}}` at all. Only an
ingredient does. That is why a fork, or two recipes with the same name,
cannot leak each other's secrets.

A slug follows `{action}-{entity}-{platform}`. The platform always goes last
(`deal-reader-hubspot`, `search-exa`). The fields `name`, `description`,
`tags`, `use_cases`, and `entity_types` are for the marketplace to show. The
engine ignores them. The `execution_scope` field is optional. It narrows
where the ingredient may run. It must stay inside what its kind already
allows. A `dom` ingredient cannot claim it can run on the server.
