- [Connections](../guides/connections.md) — the saved connections that
  wrappers use.
- [Authoring ingredient packs](../guides/authoring-ingredient-packs.md) — how
  to build, check, preview, and install these operations in the Kitchen.
- [Publishing](../guides/publishing.md) — how to publish the pack that holds
  your ingredient.

A pack is the box Recued installs. Its manifest is the list on the box. It
names the recipes and other capabilities that arrive together. It pins every version
it points at. And it holds the notes people see before they install. When
you install a pack, those files are copied to your server. The publisher
gets no ongoing control over the install after that.

Use `manifest_version: 2` for new packs. Version 1 still works for older
packs that hold only recipes.

Here is the smallest useful app pack:

```json
{
  "manifest_version": 2,
  "artifact_type": "pack",
  "pack_kind": "app_pack",
  "service_kind": "workflow",
  "slug": "sales-review",
  "publisher": "your-handle",
  "name": "Sales Review",
  "description": "Reads CRM opportunities and prepares a weekly review for the owner.",
  "version": 1,
  "contents": [
    {
      "type": "ingredient",
      "slug": "crm-opportunity-reader",
      "version": 2,
      "role": "operation_wrapper"
    },
    {
      "type": "recipe",
      "slug": "weekly-sales-review",
      "version": 1,
      "visible": true
    }
  ],
  "requires": ["install_bulk_pack"],
  "tags": ["pack:sales-review", "crm", "weekly-review"]
}
```

This example pins one ingredient and one recipe. It grants nothing by itself.
The install screen still asks the owner three things. Which connection? Which
access tier? And who may use the pack?

The envelope is the outer part of the pack file. These fields are required.
The `tags` field is not required, but you should set it:

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `manifest_version` | Yes | `1` for a pack that holds only recipes. `2` for typed `contents` and `dependencies`. |
| `slug` | Yes | The pack's name in a web address. Use small letters, numbers, and hyphens. It must start and end with a letter or a number. |
| `publisher` | Yes | Your publisher handle. A public pack is shown as `publisher/slug`. |
| `name` | Yes | The name people see in Discover and in the install dialog. |
| `description` | Yes | What the pack does, and what kind of data it touches. An empty string is allowed, but it helps nobody. |
| `version` | Yes | A whole number above zero. Raise it when the contents change, or when the install works differently. |
| `requires` | Yes | The permissions the pack asks for. It must include `install_bulk_pack`. |
| `tags` | Recommended | Words for search and grouping. Leave the list out, and you get a warning. |

| Field | Required | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `repo` | No | An HTTPS link to the source code or the support page. |
| `artifact_type` | No | If you set it, it must be `pack`. |
| `pack_kind` | No | `recipe_pack`, `app_pack`, or `foundation_pack`. |
| `service_kind` | No | What kind of service the pack adds. See the table below. |

The pack's version is separate from the versions inside it. Say a recipe goes
from version 2 to version 3. Then you need a new recipe pin and a new pack
version.

The `service_kind` field helps Discover and the install review say what is
arriving. It does not change how an operation runs.

| Value | Use for |
| --- | --- |
| `entity_platform` | A vendor or data platform, with a catalog of records and operations. A catalog is the list of what a pack can talk to and call |
| `tool_function` | One small service you can call, such as weather or address lookups |
| `cli` | A command that runs on the server |
| `channel_door` | A chat channel, or a place where messages come in |
| `ai_connection` | A connection to an AI model provider |
| `mcp_door` | A door that AI agents reach over MCP |
| `storage` | Shared storage, or the warehouse |
| `workflow` | One or more recipes that get a job done |

Version 1 needs a `recipes` list with at least one entry. It allows at most
50 recipe entries.

```json
{
  "manifest_version": 1,
  "slug": "personal-review",
  "publisher": "your-handle",
  "name": "Personal Review",
  "description": "Installs the weekly review and its two quiet data producers.",
  "version": 1,
  "recipes": [
    { "slug": "collect-review-signals", "version": 1 },
    { "slug": "refresh-review-rollup", "version": 1 },
    { "slug": "weekly-review", "version": 2 }
  ],
  "requires": ["install_bulk_pack"],
  "tags": ["pack:personal-review", "weekly-review"]
}
```

Recipes install in the order you list them. It helps to list the recipes that
pull in data, and the ones that make facts, before the recipes that use them.
That also makes the pack easier to review. Version 1 ignores `contents` and
`dependencies`, with a warning. Move to version 2 before you use either
field.

Version 2 allows up to 100 entries in `contents`. It needs at least one entry
in `contents`, or in the older `recipes` list. A pack that adds no recipes, only
capabilities, does not need a recipe at all.

| `type` | Required fields | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `recipe` | `slug`, `version` | Pins one recipe. The optional `visible` flag says if people see it as a recipe. |
| `ingredient` | One addressing form below | Pins a published ingredient, or an ingredient id under a publisher. |
| `operation_group` | `ingredient_id`, `group_id` | Adds a declared group of operations from an ingredient. |
| `channel_binding` | `channel_name`, `capability`, `bound_to_catalog`, `conversation_policy` | Connects a channel to a catalog. |
| `policy` | `policy_id` | Adds a named policy. |
| `composition` | `composition` | Holds a whole composition, written out in full. |

An ingredient entry has exactly one of these two forms:

```json
{ "type": "ingredient", "slug": "mail-reader", "version": 2, "role": "operation_wrapper" }
```

```json
{ "type": "ingredient", "ingredient_id": "recued-core/mail", "ingredient_version": 2 }
```

On the slug form, you can skip the role. If you set it, it is
`entity_schema`, `operation_wrapper`, or `producer`. Never mix the two forms
in one entry.

A recipe may appear in both `contents` and the version-2 `recipes` list.
Recued drops exact copies, where the `slug` and the `version` are both the
same. The `contents` entry wins, so its `visible` setting is kept. Better:
keep one list. Put new version-2 recipe pins in `contents`.

Most vendor packs carry one `composition` entry. A composition is written out
in full, right inside the pack. It holds flat `ingredients` and `operations`
tables. It can also hold recipe templates, default grants, work-entity
Sources (synced lists of things like tasks or deals), and recipes. Recued
checks it and breaks it down into the same ingredient and operation records
that files you publish on their own would make.

Each operation says three things. How risky is it? When does it ask for
approval? Is it safe to repeat? It also lists its arguments. Each argument
says if it is required, and if it picks the target. And each operation has a
binding that says how to run it. The binding's shape depends on the surface.
It can be an HTTP method and path template. It can be a GraphQL document. Or
it can be an argument list for a local command.

section: Where to start with a composition
body:
**Start with the [Pack editor](../guides/authoring-ingredient-packs.md).**
Point it at an API description or a command. It works out the bindings. It
shows you the risk and data review. And it refuses mixes that would be
rejected later. Most authors need nothing else.

Are you **generating** a pack instead of filling in a form? Maybe from an API
description, a script, or your own tool. Then read
[Composition](composition.md). It spells out the tables. It also says what
publishing checks, and what it does not check.

The pack parser checks the `composition` marker. Then the authoring validator
checks the composition itself. So a pack file that passes the outer check is
not proof that its composition can be published. A composition is broken
down into operation and catalog fields. See the
[ingredient manifest](ingredient-manifest.md) for those fields.

Version 2 can name packs or ingredients that must be installed first. You can
skip `min_version`. If you set it, it must be a whole number above zero.

```json
"dependencies": [
  { "type": "pack", "slug": "email-outbox-pack", "min_version": 3 },
  { "type": "ingredient", "slug": "contact-search", "min_version": 2 },
  { "type": "ingredient", "ingredient_id": "recued-core/calendar" }
]
```

An ingredient entry here uses either `slug` or `ingredient_id`. Never both.
The outer check only looks at this shape. At install time, Recued walks the
list of packs, and their lists, and so on. A missing pack, a wrong version,
or a loop fails the preflight check (the checks run before anything is
installed). An ingredient entry here only says
"this must be there first". It does not add the ingredient. Use `contents` or
a composition for that.

The pack file says what the install screen must show for review. It cannot
skip that review.

- `requires` must include `install_bulk_pack`. The needs of each recipe
  inside are added to the list. The pack cannot hide them.
- Operation risk, approval, and editable arguments come from the ingredients
  or the composition the pack points at. The owner picks the access tier and
  the audience at install time.
- `webhook_requirements` may ask for named webhook slots. Each slot must be
  backed by a webhook profile Recued knows. An author cannot put a verifier
  secret (the secret used to prove a webhook is real) or any incoming URL in
  this field.
- `mcp_body_visibility_grants` is a closed list. It is for very private
  access to message bodies. An unknown value is refused.

Some fields are for Recued's own release and set-up plumbing. A third-party
pack cannot set `pre_install: true`. It cannot set a non-empty
`connection_requirements` either. Those would let a pack install itself, or
write a form that asks for a secret key. The fields `launch_flag` and
`post_substrate_canary` are first-party rollout data. They are not feature
flags for pack authors.

The `transactional_offer` field is special too. It can describe one paid
workflow with six stages. It is allowed only on a version-2 `app_pack` with
`service_kind: "workflow"`. It is only data for the marketplace to show. The
price, the proof of payment, customer access, and delivery live elsewhere.
See [Selling access](../guides/selling-access.md).

Before you submit a pack, check all of these:

1. Every slug is lowercase and safe for a web address. Every version is a
   whole number above zero.
2. Every recipe and ingredient pin points at the publisher and version you
   meant.
3. `requires` includes `install_bulk_pack`. The install preview names every
   extra permission.
4. The `description` says what the pack does. It says which systems the pack
   touches. And it says if anything runs quietly in the background.
5. A version-2 ingredient entry uses one form. An entry in `dependencies`
   uses one form.
6. A composition written out in full passes both its authoring check and its
   break-down (decomposition) check.
7. The install preview shows the connections, operations, approvals, body
   access, webhook slots, and audience choices you expect.
8. Install and uninstall the pack on a clean server. Then look at recipes,
   grants, dependencies, and inventory. Nothing should be left behind or
   put off.

The schema check is only the first gate. Publishing checks the outer part and
every composition written out in full. It does not prove that each pinned
recipe or ingredient can be fetched when someone installs the pack. The install finds the
pinned recipes. Then it checks the packs it needs and its permissions before
it starts. If a recipe write fails, all the recipe writes roll back together.
Composition and inventory setup have their own results. So a pack file that
parses is not proof of a complete install.

This page is a short list of the main recipe fields. It is for people who write
recipes. Want the story version first? Read
[Authoring recipes](../guides/authoring-recipes.md).

The envelope is the outer shell of a recipe. Here is one with the fields this
page covers:

```json
{
  "recipe_id": "detect-deal-risk-hubspot",
  "version": 1,
  "ttl": 600,
  "metadata": {},
  "variables": {},
  "requires": [],
  "depends_on": [],
  "chat_exposed": false,
  "trigger": [],
  "event_triggers": [],
  "webhook_triggers": [],
  "auto_run": null,
  "trigger_steps": null,
  "run_mode": null,
  "provenance": true,
  "prefetch_steps": [],
  "steps": [],
  "output": {}
}
```

| Field | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `recipe_id` | string | The recipe's name. Its shape is `{action}-{entity}-{qualifier}[-{platform}]`. The platform always goes last |
| `version` | number | A whole number. It says which version of this recipe this is |
| `ttl` | number | How many seconds a fetched answer may be kept and reused. It is the default for ingredient fetches |
| `metadata` | object | Display and marketplace fields. See the table below |
| `variables` | object | Values the user can set. Steps read them as `{{config.*}}` |
| `requires` | string[] | Permissions the recipe needs, such as `notification_send` or `mail_send` |
| `depends_on` | string[] | Packs whose operations the steps call. Write each one as `publisher.pack`. Built-in `core.*` operations need no entry |
| `chat_exposed` | boolean | Let chat and connected AI agents use this recipe as a tool. See [Exposing recipes to chat](../guides/exposing-recipes-to-chat.md) |

section: Envelope fields for triggers, steps, and output
body:
| Field | Type | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `trigger` | string[] | URL patterns of the web pages this recipe is made for. Leave it out, and the recipe runs by hand only |
| `event_triggers` | object[] | Warehouse events (a record in your warehouse changing) that start the recipe. See [Triggers and watchers](../guides/authoring-triggers.md) |
| `webhook_triggers` | object[] | Incoming webhooks that start the recipe. Each one names a verification profile (the named way the sender proves the message is real) |
| `auto_run` | object | Makes the recipe tick by itself: `{ "interval_ms": 60000, "dynamic": false }` |
| `trigger_steps` | step[] | Steps that run before each tick and decide if the tick goes on. Needs `auto_run` |
| `run_mode` | string | `live`, `backfill`, or `manual`. It tags the audit entries |
| `provenance` | boolean | Default `true`. It writes the links that timelines are built from |
| `prefetch_steps` | step[] | Steps that all run at the same time, before the main steps |
| `steps` | step[] | The main steps. They run one after another |
| `output` | object | The `render` sections. They send step results to the screen |

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `name`, `description` | What people see: the name, and what the recipe does |
| `author` | The publisher handle. That is your name in the marketplace |
| `tags` | Any words you like. They help people find and filter recipes |
| `supported_platforms` | The platforms this copy of the recipe is made for |
| `variant_group` | Groups the copies of one recipe made for different platforms |
| `execution_scope` | You can skip it. It narrows where the recipe may run. It must stay inside what the ingredient kinds already allow |
| `budget_ms` | The most time a run may take, in milliseconds. The engine stops a run that goes past it. Set one on everything you ship |
| `fork_of` | Where a published fork came from: the original recipe, its author, and its version |

```json
{
  "id": "risky",
  "transform": "filter",
  "array": "{{step.deals}}",
  "field": "stage",
  "operator": "equal",
  "value": "at_risk",
  "skip_when": "{{step.deals}} is_empty"
}
```

Recued tells the kind of step from which field is present:

| Kind | Field | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Transform | `transform` | A pure local function. Its settings sit right on the step. See [Transforms](transforms.md) |
| Ingredient | `ingredient` | A declared operation: HTTP, DOM, AI, chat, MCP, service, storage, or connection. Its settings go under `input`, with dotted keys such as `llm.data` |
| Operation | `op` | A named operation. It is built in (`core.mail.get`, `core.notification.send`, `core.watch.time`, …) or it comes from an installed pack (`publisher.pack.entity.verb`, listed in `depends_on`). Its arguments go under `args`. The account it uses goes under `connection`, usually `"{{config.<your connection variable>}}"` |
| Guard | `guard` | The field holds a condition. When the condition is true, the recipe stops |
| Condition | `condition` | Checks a condition. Then it runs the `then` steps or the `else` steps |

Every step runs the same way:

```text
skip_when? → compute → step.<id> = result → fail_on?
```

- If `skip_when` is true, the step stores `null`. The recipe goes on.
- `fail_on` is checked after the step computes. If it is true, the recipe
  stops.
- `foreach` runs the step once for each item in a list. Inside, `{{item.*}}`
  is that item. The output is one envelope per item:
  `{ ok, result?, error?, item }`. They keep the input's order.
- A prefetch step can also say `"optional": true`. Then a failure stores
  `null` instead of stopping the run.

Trigger steps (`trigger_steps`) have the same shape. Every one must return
`should_run: true`, or the tick stops. Their outputs land on
`{{trigger.<id>.*}}` for the steps after them.

A variable has two forms. A **bare value** is a setting you tuned. Recued
works out its type. The one-time run form does not ask about it. An
**object** is a question for the person who runs the recipe. It gets its own
box on that form.

```json
"variables": {
  "recipient":  { "label": "Send to", "type": "text" },
  "window":     { "label": "Window", "type": "enum", "options": ["7d", "30d"] },
  "max_rows":   50,
  "deal_id":    null
}
```

| Bare value | Inferred | Control |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `50` | number | A number box |
| `true` / `false` | boolean | An on/off switch |
| `"text"` | string | A text box |
| `["a", "b"]` | enum | A drop-down list. The first one is the default |
| `null` | string, **required** | A text box with no default. The recipe cannot run until you fill it in |

You can still change a tuned setting in the places where tuning belongs.
Those are the install dialog, the recipe editor, and the Schedule and Trigger
tabs. There, "run every night with `window: 30d`" is a real setup choice. Only
the one-time run form stops asking.

These are the only fields there are. **Any other field is refused when you
install.** So a made-up field fails loudly. It is never quietly ignored.

| Field | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `label` | **Required.** The words shown. It also tells Recued this is a question, not a setting |
| `type` | **Required.** A string that is not empty. See the table below |
| `optional` | `true` lets the person leave it empty. **Leave it out to require a value** |
| `default` | Used when nothing is given |
| `help` | One line of help under the box |
| `link` | A web link to more help |
| `options` | For `type: "enum"`. The choices. The first one is the default |
| `provider`, `scopes` | For `type: "oauth"`. Which broker handles the sign-in, and which scopes to ask for |
| `accept_mime_types` | For `type: "file_ref"`. It only narrows the file picker. It is not a safety wall |
| `connection_kind` | For `type: "connection"`. One of `api`, `mcp`, or `notification` |
| `variant_group` | For `type: "service_ref"`. Which family of set-up services the picker shows |

There is no `required` field. The `optional` field is the one that exists.
Leave it out, and the value is already required. There is no `pattern` field either.
To check the *shape* of a value, use a `guard` step. A variable says what a
value is called and how to collect it. It never says what counts as valid.

The field list is closed, but `type` is open. These types each get their own
kind of box:

`text` · `number` · `boolean` · `enum` (with `options`) · `datetime` · `date` ·
`url` · `secret` · `oauth` · `file_slug` · `file_ref` · `file_ref[]`

`datetime` is one moment. The form sends it with the time zone of the person
filling it in, like `2026-10-01T09:30:00+02:00`. `date` is a day, like
`2026-10-01`. It has no time and no time zone. Use it for a due date or a target
date.

These are allowed too, and many recipes use them. `connection` and
`service_ref` get their own pickers. The rest show as a plain text box:

`string` · `array` · `object` · `json` · `connection` · `service_ref`

`string` is the most common type in shipped recipes. It works like `text`.
Any other non-empty string installs and shows as text. So the list can grow,
and the recipes you already published still work. That is why an unknown
*type* is allowed but an unknown *field* is not. A type has a safe fallback.
A field nobody reads has none.

section: A caller may only pass what you declared
body:
A chat request, an MCP call, a button, or a schedule can pass values to your
recipe. If it uses a name that is not in `variables`, the run is **refused**.
The name is not ignored. So declare every argument you want to accept. And
remove any old name you no longer read.

Give a `default` only when a good one exists. A required input with a filler
default is not really required. An empty string, a zero, or an empty list is a
filler. The caller can leave it out, and the recipe runs with the filler.

```text
"literal"              → use as-is
"{{ref}}"              → resolve, preserve type
"{{ref:format}}"       → resolve; the hint applies only during interpolation
"text {{ref}} text"    → interpolate → string
10, true, false        → native JSON type
null                   → required from caller
```

The format hints are `:currency`, `:number`, `:date`, `:relative`, and
`:percent`.

A condition is a short string. One condition per field. One operator per
condition. Plain values have no quotes: write `equal closed_won`, never
`equal 'closed_won'`.

| Operator | Form |
| --- | --- |
| `equal`, `not_equal` | two sides (binary) |
| `greater`, `greater_or_equal`, `less`, `less_or_equal` | two sides (binary) |
| `is_null`, `is_not_null`, `is_empty`, `is_not_empty` | one side (unary) |
| `contains`, `not_contains` | two sides (binary) |
| `in`, `not_in` | two sides, and the right side is a list. Use the object form |

The object form, for a list value:

```json
{ "field": "{{step.x}}", "operator": "in", "value": ["a", "b"] }
```

Want to join conditions? Use a transform step, `any` or `all`. It stores a
true or false. Check that. There is no `and` or `or` inside a condition
string.

A namespace is the first part of a `{{ref}}`. It says where the value comes
from.

| Namespace | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `config` | The recipe's variables. They are set at install or at run time |
| `context` | Facts about the caller, plus fields the engine adds (see below) |
| `meta` | The recipe's metadata |
| `step` | Every step's output, both prefetch and main steps |
| `trigger` | The trigger steps' outputs, on recipes that tick by themselves |
| `item` | The current item inside a `foreach` |
| `shared` | Records you can write that live in the cache |
| `data.shared` | Records you can write that are kept for good |
| `data.memory` | Audit and memory entries. Needs the read-memory permission |
| `data.contact` | Your contacts. Each one is keyed by its main email address |
| `connection` | The non-secret fields of named connections |

Only ingredients may use `{{vault.*}}`. A recipe never sees a secret key. The
vendor aliases `data.hubspot.*`, `data.salesforce.*`, and `data.crm.*` read
enrichments on CRM records. They work with fixed ids only.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `context.tabs` | The ingredient slugs whose URL patterns match a browser tab that is open |
| `context.server` | `{ available, name? }`. Can the paired server be reached right now? |
| `context.event` | The event that fired the recipe, on a reactive run (a run started by an event, not by you). On updates, `payload.prev` holds the old values of the hot fields (the fields that change most) |
| `context.recipe.*` | Step results saved from the last run, so one run can pick up from the one before. Not set on the first run |

Each transform's settings are listed in the
[transforms reference](transforms.md). Tier 1 is the small building blocks:

| Group | Transforms |
| --- | --- |
| Collection | filter, sort, map, reduce, unique, flatten, slice, group_by, to_list, partition |
| Object | merge, pick, omit, rename, set |
| String | lowercase, uppercase, trim, split, concat, replace, template, truncate, strip_html |
| Numeric | round, clamp, to_number, math, weighted_score |
| Date | date_diff, date_format, date_add, date_parse, is_past, is_future, date_period |
| Logic | compare, coalesce, switch, all, any, count, default, not, ternary, pluralize |
| Boolean | starts_with, ends_with |
| Privacy | hash_replace, hash_restore, redact |
| Display | to_checklist, to_table, to_summary, to_csv |

Tier 2 is handy shortcuts built from Tier 1: find, pluck, sum, min_by, max_by,
percent, join, and group_by with aggregate.

Two modes are worth knowing. The `filter` transform takes
`mode: "all" | "any"` plus a `conditions` list. That checks many conditions in
one step. The `map` transform takes an `expression` over `{{item.*}}`. The
expression can be one ref, a math expression, or an object template. Add
`output_field` to attach the answer to each item instead of replacing the
item.

| Function | Input | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ai-classify` | `llm.data`, `llm.categories[]`, `llm.context?` | `{ category, confidence, reasoning }` |
| `ai-score` | `llm.data`, `llm.criteria[]`, `llm.scale?` | `{ score, breakdown[], reasoning }` |
| `ai-extract` | `llm.data`, `llm.fields[]` | `{ [field]: value }` |
| `ai-summarize` | `llm.data`, `llm.max_length?`, `llm.focus?` | `{ summary, key_points[] }` |
| `ai-sentiment` | `llm.data` | `{ sentiment, score, signals[] }` |
| `ai-compare` | `llm.data_a`, `llm.data_b`, `llm.dimensions[]?` | `{ differences[], similarities[], recommendation }` |
| `ai-generate` | `llm.data`, `llm.template_type`, `llm.tone?` | `{ content }` |
| `ai-translate` | `llm.data`, `llm.target_language` | `{ translated, source_language, confidence }` |
| `ai-rewrite` | `llm.data`, `llm.style`, `llm.instructions?` | `{ rewritten }` |
| `ai-prompt` | `llm.system_prompt`, `llm.prompt`, `llm.output_format?`, `llm.model_hint?`, `llm.allow_search?` | uncontracted |

Batch mode: every function except `ai-compare` can take a list as `llm.data`,
plus a non-empty `llm.id_field`. That is one model call. It gives back one
answer per item, in the same order as the input. Each answer is the source
record merged with the result fields. The model hints are `fast`, `quality`,
and `thinking`.

```json
"output": {
  "render": [
    { "type": "summary", "source": "step.overview", "label": "Overview" },
    { "type": "ai_analysis", "source": "step.analysis" }
  ]
}
```

This only routes. There is no logic here. A null source is not shown. The
section types:

| Type | Renders |
| --- | --- |
| `checklist` | The output of `to_checklist`, as pass, fail, or neutral items |
| `table` | The output of `to_table`, as a table |
| `summary` | The output of `to_summary`, as label and value pairs |
| `ai_analysis` | An AI answer, with a badge that shows how sure it is |
| `text` | Any string |
| `copyable` | A string with a copy button |
| `button` | Buttons the owner clicks. Each one opens a normal recipe run, with all the usual checks |
| `file_artifact` | One or more file cards. You must be signed in to preview or download |
| `link_button` | A plain link out: a label plus an HTTPS URL. It is the one block a public page for visitors can act on |
| `json` | Raw data from a step. It is the detail behind a tidy card. Each surface shows it its own way: the web folds it up, a chat or agent caller gets it word for word |
| `filter` | A form built from your declared variables. Submit it, and the whole recipe runs again with those values. Owner only. A page for visitors leaves this block out |

`render` is the **only** way a run's data reaches anyone. A step result that
is not sent to a section cannot be seen. Not by a person. Not by a model. Use
`json` when a reader needs to check the work behind a summary.

The `filter` block is the one section that is not `{ type, source, label }`.
It also has three more fields: `fields`, `hidden`, and `submit`. The `fields`
list names the declared variable keys to show as boxes. The `hidden` list
names declared keys that are sent on submit but never shown. A paging cursor
(a marker for the next page of results) is the usual one. The `submit` field is the button text. Every box comes from
the variable's own declaration. There is no styling to write.

When a recipe is refused, Recued names what it did not like. Here are the
ones authors meet most:

| Refusal | Cause |
| --- | --- |
| `output_unknown_key`, `output_section_unknown_key` | A made-up field on `output` or on a section. `label` is the display field. There is no `title`, `content`, or `body` |
| `variable_hint_invalid` | An object-form variable with no `label` or no `type`, or an empty one |
| `variable_hint_unknown_key` | A field on a variable that does not exist. Most often it is `required`, which was never a field |
| `undeclared_variable_ref` | The recipe reads `{{config.x}}`, but there is no `x` in `variables` |
| `undeclared_config_argument` | A caller sent a config key the recipe never declared. This happens at run time, not at install |
| `unknown_transform` | A transform name Recued does not know |
| `condition_operator_invalid` | An operator that is not one of the fourteen |
| `forward_step_ref` | A step reads a step that runs later |
| `nested_template` | A `{{ }}` inside another `{{ }}` |
| `context_recipe_in_auto_run` | `{{context.recipe.*}}` in a recipe that ticks by itself. It carries last-run state on manual and scheduled runs only |
| `filter_variable_undeclared`, `filter_field_not_labeled` | A `filter` block names a key that is not declared, or one that is a bare setting instead of a labelled question |

`orphan_step` and `ttl_below_floor` are warnings, not refusals. The first is a
step nothing reads. The second is a cache TTL that is lower than the practical
floor.

```text
Recipe:      {action}-{entity}-{qualifier}-{platform}    detect-deal-risk-hubspot
Ingredient:  {action}-{entity}-{platform}                deal-reader-hubspot
AI:          ai-{function}                               ai-score
Vendor:      {action}-{vendor}                           search-exa
```

The platform always goes last. That is what lets `variant_group` fold the
copies made for different platforms into one marketplace card.

A transform is a small safe tool. It makes a new value and touches nothing
else. It runs inside your server, with no call to the internet. It costs
nothing. The same input always gives the same answer.

The settings of a transform sit **flat on the step**. They sit right next to
`id`, `transform`, `skip_when`, and `fail_on`. There is no extra box around
them. Use the setting names below exactly as written. A `?` at the end of a
name means you can leave that setting out. The ref `{{item.*}}` only works
inside `map` expressions and inside `foreach` loops.

```json
{ "id": "days", "transform": "date_diff",
  "from": "{{step.deal.last_activity_date}}", "to": "now", "unit": "days" }
```

A collection is a list of items (an array). These tools work on lists.

| Transform | Parameters | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `filter` | `array`, `field`, `operator`, `value?` — or `conditions[]` with `mode?` (`all`/`any`) | array |
| `sort` | `array`, `fields[]` of `{ field, direction }` | array |
| `map` | `array`, `expression` — or `apply` + the applied transform's params; `output_field?` | array |
| `reduce` | `array`, `field`, `operator`, `initial?` | value |
| `find` | `array`, `field`, `operator`, `value` | the first item that matches |
| `pluck` | `array`, `field` | array of values |
| `sum` | `array`, `field` | number |
| `min_by` / `max_by` | `array`, `field` | one item |
| `unique` | `array`, `field` | array |
| `flatten` | `array`, `depth` | array |
| `slice` | `array`, `start`, `end` | array |
| `group_by` | `array`, `field`, `aggregate?` | object — or an array when you use `aggregate` |
| `partition` | the same parameters as `filter` | `{ matched, unmatched }` |
| `to_list` | `input` (an object) | array of `{ key, value }` |
| `count` | `input` | number |
| `join` | `array`, `separator` | string |
| `enrich_by` | `array`, `with`, `key`, `with_key?`, `fields?`, `prefix?` | array — each item is joined to its match in `with`, using the key |

`reduce` can use these operators: `sum`, `count`, `avg`, `min`, `max`,
`concat`, `or`, `and`.

`filter` can take many conditions at once. By default all of them must be
true (AND). Set `mode: "any"` and one true condition is enough (OR).

`map` has three kinds of expression:

- One ref. It pulls out that value and keeps its type.
- A math expression over `{{item.*}}`. It can use `+ - * / %`, `min`,
  `max`, `abs`, `ceil`, `floor`, and `round`.
- An object template.

`output_field` adds the answer to each item. Without it, the answer replaces
the item:

```json
{ "id": "weighted", "transform": "map", "array": "{{step.deals}}",
  "expression": "{{item.amount}} * {{item.stage_probability}} / 100",
  "output_field": "weighted_amount" }
```

`group_by` with `aggregate` works out numbers for each group. It returns an
array:

```json
{ "id": "by_stage", "transform": "group_by",
  "array": "{{step.deals}}", "field": "stage",
  "aggregate": {
    "count": { "operator": "count" },
    "total": { "field": "amount", "operator": "sum" }
  } }
```

Without `aggregate` it returns `{ key: [items] }`. To walk through the
groups, chain `to_list` and then `map`.

| Transform | Parameters | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `merge` | `sources[]`, `strategy` (`shallow` / `deep` / `concat`) | object |
| `pick` | `source` (ref) + `fields[]` — or `source` as an object template | object |
| `omit` | `source`, `fields[]` | object |
| `rename` | `source`, `mapping` (old → new) | object |
| `set` | `source`, `field`, `value` | object |
| `prefix_keys` | `source`, `prefix` | object with every key prefixed |
| `project` | `object`, `expression` (an object template) | one record, reshaped. It is `map` for a single object |

| Transform | Parameters | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `template` | `template` (a string with `{{refs}}`) | string |
| `concat` | `values[]` | string |
| `split` | `input`, `delimiter` | array |
| `replace` | `input`, `pattern`, `replacement`, `all` | string |
| `truncate` | `input`, `max_length`, `suffix` | string |
| `strip_html` | `input` | plain-text string |
| `lowercase` / `uppercase` / `trim` | `input` | string |
| `starts_with` / `ends_with` | `input`, `prefix` / `suffix` | boolean |
| `contains_any` | `input`, `terms[]`, `case_sensitive` | boolean: true if any term appears |
| `string_length` | `input` | the number of characters |
| `sha256` | `input` | hex digest (a fixed-length fingerprint written in hex). Use it to make a stable id from your inputs |
| `encode_base64` / `decode_base64` | `input` | string |

These help in two cases. Some operations have a size limit. And sometimes
you need an id that is always the same, so a re-run repeats the work instead
of making a copy.

| Transform | Parameters | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `json_stringify` | `input` | JSON string |
| `json_parse` | `input` | parsed value |
| `json_byte_length` | `input` | the size of the value as JSON, in bytes |
| `utf8_byte_length` | `input` | the size of a string in UTF-8 (the usual text encoding), in bytes |

| Transform | Parameters | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `to_number` | `input` | number |
| `math` | `left`, `operator`, `right?` | number |
| `round` | `input`, `precision` | number |
| `clamp` | `input`, `min`, `max` | number |
| `percent` | `value`, `total`, `precision` | decimal (show it with `:percent`) |
| `weighted_score` | `scores[]` of `{ value, weight }`, `clamp?` `[min, max]`, `precision?` | number |

`math` can use `add`, `subtract`, `multiply`, `divide`, and `modulo`. It can
also use `abs`, `ceil`, and `floor`. Those three take one number only.

| Transform | Parameters | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `date_diff` | `from`, `to` (accepts `"now"`), `unit` | number |
| `date_format` | `date`, `format` | string |
| `date_add` | `date`, `amount`, `unit` | ISO 8601 string |
| `date_parse` | `input`, `input_format` | ISO 8601 string |
| `is_past` / `is_future` | `date` | boolean |
| `date_period` | `period` | `{ start, end }` ISO strings |

Units are `days`, `hours`, `minutes`, and `seconds`.

`date_period` takes one of these names:

`today`, `yesterday`, `this_week`, `last_week`, `this_month`, `last_month`,
`this_quarter`, `last_quarter`, `this_year`, `last_year`, `last_7_days`,
`last_30_days`, `last_90_days`, `next_7_days`, `next_30_days`.

The start day and the end day are both included. Days are in UTC (world
clock time). Weeks are ISO weeks (weeks start on Monday). The period comes
from the run's own clock. So one run gets one fixed answer, and running it
again gives that same answer.

### Timestamps

| Transform | Parameters | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `to_recent_date` | `input` (a number) | The value turned into Unix milliseconds (milliseconds since 1970), or `null` when it is not a recent timestamp. Check the result with `is_null`. It never guesses |

| Transform | Parameters | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `compare` | `left`, `operator` (any of the 14), `right?` | boolean |
| `any` / `all` | `values[]` (booleans) — or `conditions[]` (condition strings) | boolean |
| `coalesce` | `values[]` | the first value that is not null |
| `default` | `value`, `fallback` | the value, or the fallback when it is null or an empty string |
| `not` | `input` | the opposite boolean |
| `ternary` | `if`, `then`, `else?` | one of two values |
| `switch` | `input`, `cases` (map), `default` | the mapped value |
| `pluralize` | `count`, `zero?`, `one`, `many` | the chosen text |

`default` treats an empty string as missing. It keeps `0` and `false`. Use it
instead of `coalesce` when a template might turn into `""`.

| Transform | Parameters | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `hash_replace` | `data`, `fields[]` | `{ data, mapping }` |
| `hash_restore` | `data`, `mapping` | the restored object or string |
| `redact` | `data`, `fields[]` (paths, `[*]` allowed), `marker` | the object with those fields blacked out |

Use `hash_replace` before an AI step. Use `hash_restore` after it. That way
the AI model never sees the fields you chose. The mapping never leaves the
run.

| Transform | Parameters | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `to_checklist` | `title`, `items[]` | checklist object |
| `to_table` | `array`, `columns[]` of `{ field, label, format? }` | table object |
| `to_summary` | `fields[]` of `{ label, value }` | summary object |
| `to_csv` | `array`, `columns?`, `header?`, `delimiter?` | CSV string |
| `to_slack_blocks` | `blocks[]` | a Slack Block Kit (Slack's message layout format) payload, for a notification step that posts to Slack |

A checklist item looks like `{ label, issue, detail_ok, detail_issue, detail_null }`.
`issue` is a condition string. True shows as a problem. False shows as fine.
Null shows as unknown.

A table column can have one of these formats: `text`, `currency`, `number`,
`date`, `relative_date`, `boolean`, `percent`.

A checklist item or a table column with `type: "action"` can carry an action.
An action always shows as a button the owner clicks. The click opens a
normal recipe run. All the usual rules and approvals still apply. An action
never runs on its own.

`to_csv` escapes text the way RFC 4180 (the standard CSV rules) says. Pair it with a file write. Then
you get a file a spreadsheet can open.

An enrichment is a fact Recued works out ahead of time and sticks onto a
record. The `enrichment-or-fetch` transform reads one. It returns the stored
fact when one exists, is fresh, and is trusted enough. If not, it tells your fallback step
to fetch a fresh one.

| Parameter | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `ref` | The dotted enrichment ref, such as `data.contact.{{step.email}}.company_summary` |
| `trust_min?` | The lowest confidence you accept (default 0.8) |
| `max_age_ms?` | Reject rows older than this |
| `fallback_step?` | The step to jump to on a miss |

It returns `{ value, source, confidence?, fallback? }`. `source` is one of
`enrichment`, `miss`, `stale`, `low_trust`, `unparseable_ref`, or
`no_runtime`.

- [Recipe schema](recipe-schema.md): the steps these tools run inside.
- [Authoring recipes](../guides/authoring-recipes.md): when to use a
  transform and when to use an AI step.

Recued comes with no AI model of its own. So setting up AI means telling
Recued which AI services to send calls to. Everything is on one page:
**Settings → AI/Models**. You can start for free. Add paid keys only if you
want them.

An API key is a secret code that lets your server use an AI service. Add
your own free-tier keys from Groq, OpenRouter, Gemini, Cerebras, GitHub
Models, and Mistral. Recued spreads calls across them. It stays inside each
provider's free limit. This is the usual workhorse. It gives structured
output. It works with no screen. And it costs nothing until a free limit
runs out.

Add one under **Settings → AI/Models → Providers → Free pool**. Choose its
protocol: most free tiers are OpenAI-compatible, with the provider's base
URL. Then enter the model and the key. **Test connection** tries it before
you add it. Leave the name blank and it is named from the address, such as
`groq`. You can edit, disable, test, or remove each one later. An edit keeps
the saved key unless you change the protocol or the base URL.

Two slots hold paid or self-hosted models:

- **Slot 1 (fast)** — the model for daily work.
- **Slot 2 (quality)** — the model for harder questions. It is also used for
  extended thinking.

Set them up under **Settings → AI/Models → Providers**. The first-run
**Set up Chat** form names OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini. For anything else,
its **Set up slot 1 and slot 2** link opens that tab.

Each slot asks for:

- **Provider**: your own name for the service, such as "Groq". It is only a
  label.
- **Protocol**: how Recued talks to it. Choose OpenAI, Anthropic, Google
  Gemini, or OpenAI-compatible. OpenAI-compatible covers Groq, OpenRouter,
  Mistral, and a local Ollama or vLLM server. Use a local one if you want AI
  that never leaves your own machines.
- **Model** and **API key**. A local model that needs no key takes any word,
  such as `none`.
- **Base URL**: needed for OpenAI-compatible. The others can skip it.

A saved key stays with the protocol and base URL it was saved for. Change
either one and you enter the key again: Recued never sends a saved key to a
new address. Change only the model or the name, and the saved key is kept.

**Test connection** tries the form as it is, before you save. When something
is missing, the answer shows under the button you pressed.

An embedding turns text into a list of numbers. Some recipes need that. Set
up the **Embeddings slot** under **Providers → Embeddings** only when a
recipe or producer clearly needs vector embeddings. Take the housekeeping
producer that embeds mail. That lets semantic clustering compare messages.
The slot has its own provider, embedding model, and API key. It can also
have a base URL, which you may skip.

Recipes reach the slot through the read-only `core.ai.embed` kernel op:

```json
{
  "id": "embed",
  "op": "core.ai.embed",
  "args": {
    "llm.data": "{{step.source.text}}"
  }
}
```

The step returns `vector`, `dimensions`, and `model`. You can add an
`llm.dimensions` argument. Do that only when the chosen embedding model
accepts a dimension hint. Embeddings do not support `llm.pii_fields`. So
protect private data before you pass it in as `llm.data`.

This slot is kept apart from normal AI routing. Built-in chat never uses it.
Normal AI recipe steps never use it. And an embedding call never falls back
to the free pool or to the fast and quality slots.

A normal AI recipe asks for a kind of model: `fast`, `quality`, or
`thinking`. It never names a provider. Recued picks free sources before paid
keys. It checks what is ready before a recipe starts. So a step that cannot
be served fails right at the start. One call is one billing event.
A paid call is never quietly sent again. See
[AI and models](../concepts/ai-models.md) for the full picture.

Some enrichment topics use AI in the background. Each topic runs at the
trust level you set: off, manual, or automatic. Each topic also has a pool
policy: free sources only, paid only, or free then paid. And there is one
global Pause-AI switch. Nothing turns itself to automatic. Recued suggests.
You decide.
Try it in chat: [AI chat and MCP](../guides/ai-chat-and-mcp.md).

Your server holds a lot. It holds the warehouse and your connections. It
holds installed recipes, the audit history, and stored files. All of it can
be saved as one locked file. That file is called an archive. It can be loaded onto any
server. You do both jobs from the webclient. Neither job needs a terminal
on the server machine.

Open **Settings → Backup & Recovery**. It saves the whole server. That
means the database, the settings, the secret keys, and the stored files.
All of it goes into one `.recued.archive` file. You download it in your browser. The
export streams as it goes. So a warehouse of many gigabytes backs up fine
on a small machine. It does not run out of memory. The server CLI can also
write the archive to a path. Use that for scripted backups.

The archive is encrypted. Your recovery key is what opens it. The recovery
key is 24 secret words. Keep the archive file and the recovery key apart.
Then you hold a complete restore.

The archive holds the server as it was at export time. Anything that
happened after that is not in it. So back up on a rhythm that matches how
much you are willing to lose.

Restoring is the first thing the webclient can do on a new server. You do
not pair first and restore later. The steps:

1. Install a fresh server. Open the webclient's pair form.
2. Choose **Restore a backup**. Give it four things. The server address.
   The fresh server's pairing code. The backup's 24-word recovery key. And
   the archive file.
3. The archive uploads. Then it is checked in a dry run. Nothing is saved
   yet. Is the recovery key wrong? It just bounces back. You can try again.
   The server stays untouched.
4. Look at the preview of what the archive holds. Then confirm.
5. The restore is saved. The server restarts into the restored data. Your
   webclient reconnects, and it is already paired.

A service manager, like the start-at-login setup the install script makes,
restarts the server by itself. A server running in a plain terminal window needs starting again
by hand.

A server that is already paired and in use can also load an archive. Open
**Settings → Backup & Recovery**. Two guards apply:

- An archive from a **different server identity** does not quietly replace
  this server's data. It also needs this server's own current recovery key,
  plus a clear yes from you.
- An archive made by a **newer server version** is refused. You are told to
  update first. An archive from the same or an older version is fine. It
  is moved forward by itself at the restart.

- The archive is checked before anything that cannot be undone. The archive
  key is proven in the dry run before anything is saved.
- The restored database is put next to the live one. They are swapped in
  one move at restart. If a restore is cut off, the server starts on the
  old data, untouched.
- An upload or a save can lose its network connection. Nothing gets
  broken, and you do not have to upload again.

- [Install the server](install-server.md) — where the data directory lives.
- [Pairing and devices](pairing-and-devices.md) — the recovery key this
  flow depends on.

Your server can read your Gmail and your Google Calendar. Google has rules
for how an app gets in. The way that keeps working depends on your account.

| Your account | Mail | Calendar |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Google Workspace | A sign-in app set to Internal | The same app |
| Free Gmail, and you own a web domain | A published sign-in app | The same app |
| Free Gmail, no domain | IMAP with an app password | Not possible today |

A Google Workspace account is a work or school account. An admin runs it.

A sign-in app is a small setup you make in Google Cloud. It lets your server
sign in to your Google account. Google calls it an OAuth app.

A new sign-in app starts in test mode. Google calls it Testing. In Testing,
every sign-in stops after 7 days. Your server would stop reading your mail
each week. So never leave the app in Testing.

Out of Testing, a sign-in keeps working until you remove it. Google still
ends it in two cases: nobody uses it for six months, or you change your
Google password. Then you connect again.

This is the way for a free Gmail account with no domain. An app password is
a code of 16 characters. It lets one app read your mail. That app never sees
your real password.

1. Turn on 2-Step Verification for your Google account.
2. Make an app password at `myaccount.google.com/apppasswords`.
3. In Recued, open **Connections**, then **Mail**. Choose **Connect mailbox**,
   then **IMAP / SMTP**.
4. Fill in the form:
   - IMAP Host: `imap.gmail.com`
   - IMAP Port: `993`, with Use TLS on
   - Username: your Gmail address
   - Password: the app password
   - Folders: `INBOX, [Gmail]/Sent Mail`
5. To send mail too, set SMTP Host to `smtp.gmail.com` and SMTP Port to `465`.

Did you change your Google password? That ends every app password. Make a new
one. Some accounts do not get app passwords at all. You will not see them if
you sign in only with security keys. You will not see them with Advanced
Protection. Many work and school accounts do not have them either.

Google Calendar does not take app passwords. So this way works for mail only.

This is the way for a Google Workspace account. It covers mail and calendar.

1. Open the Google Cloud Console. Make a project, or pick one.
2. Go to **APIs & Services**, then **Library**. Turn on the Gmail API. Turn on
   the Google Calendar API too, if you want your calendar.
3. Open **Google Auth Platform**, then **Audience**. Choose **Internal**.
   There is nothing to publish. An Internal app has no Testing stage, so its
   sign-in does not stop after 7 days.
4. Go to **Credentials**. Choose **Create credentials**, then
   **OAuth client ID**, then **Web application**.
5. Under **Authorized redirect URIs**, add the callback URL that Recued shows.
   It is on the Gmail form under **Connections**.
6. Copy the Client ID and the Client secret into that form.

This is the way for a free Gmail account when you own a web domain. It covers
mail and calendar. Google only publishes the app when its details are
complete.

Make the app like the Workspace one, with these changes:

1. Under **Audience**, choose **External**.
2. Open **Branding**. Fill in the app name, your support email, and the
   developer contact. Leave the logo empty.
3. Add a home page link and a privacy policy link. Both go on your own
   domain. Add a terms link too, if you have one.
4. Add your domain under **Authorized domains**. Prove you own it in Google
   Search Console.
5. Do not add `recued.com`. You cannot prove you own it, so Google will not
   publish the app.
6. Go to **Audience** and choose **Publish app**. The status becomes In
   production.

Your home page says what the app does. For example: it lets your own server
read your own mail. Your privacy page says who uses it, and where the mail
goes. For example: only you use it, and your mail stays on your own computer.

section: Connect from the server's own address
body:
A published app works only from the server's own address. Here is why. The
page at app.recued.com sends sign-ins back through `recued.com`. Google wants
proof that you own every domain your app uses. A LAN address sends them
through `recued.com` too.

So open Recued on the server itself at `http://127.0.0.1:7717/webclient`.
Is this address new to your browser? Then pair it once, like a new device.
Connect your Google account there. Does your server have no screen? Make a
tunnel from your own computer:

```sh
ssh -L 7717:127.0.0.1:7717 you@your-server
```

Then open `http://127.0.0.1:7717/webclient` on your computer. You only
connect once. After that, the account keeps working from app.recued.com too.

At sign-in, Google shows a warning: "Google hasn't verified this app". Choose
**Advanced**. Then choose **Go to** your app's name **(unsafe)**. Google says
"unsafe" about every app it has not checked. This one is yours, and it only
talks to your own server. On the next screen, allow the access it asks for.
Up to 100 people can use an app like this.

section: Calendar without Workspace or a domain
body:
Google Calendar only lets apps in through a sign-in app. It does not take app
passwords. So a free Gmail account with no domain cannot keep Google Calendar
connected today. Mail still works, with an app password.

Google Cloud also lists a Gmail MCP API and a Google Calendar MCP API. They
use the same kind of sign-in app, so the same rules apply. They are still in
an early preview. The Gmail one can write drafts, but it cannot send mail.

- [Connections](../guides/connections.md). How a saved connection works.
- [Connect Outlook and Microsoft 365](connect-microsoft.md). The same choices
  for a Microsoft account.
- [Use Recued on another device](lan-access.md). The addresses your server
  answers on.

Your server can read your Outlook mail and calendar. It signs in through an
app that you make in Microsoft Entra. Who can make that app depends on your
account.

| Your account | Who makes the sign-in app | Who approves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Personal: Outlook.com, Hotmail or Live | You | You, when you sign in |
| Work or school: Microsoft 365 | An admin where you work or study | That admin |

A sign-in app is a small setup in Entra. Entra calls it an app registration.

There is no way in with a password. Outlook.com and Microsoft 365 no longer
let other mail apps sign in with one. So IMAP and SMTP cannot reach them.

section: Why a work account needs an admin
body:
Microsoft sets a default rule for work and school accounts. Staff may not
approve an app that reads mail or calendars. It does not matter who made the app. Only
an admin can approve it. One approval covers all staff. Your workplace may
also have its own rule.

The admin needs one of these roles:

- Global Administrator
- Privileged Role Administrator
- Cloud Application Administrator
- Application Administrator

Is the **Grant admin consent** button greyed out for you? Then you do not
hold one of these roles. That is your workplace's rule, not a fault in
Recued. Send this page to someone who holds one.

Microsoft is strict about the callback address. Two of your addresses work:

- app.recued.com.
- The server's own address, `http://localhost:7717/webclient`.

Two do not:

- A LAN address. Its callback names the page after a `?`. Microsoft does
  not allow that for an app that takes personal accounts.
- `http://127.0.0.1`. The Azure portal refuses an `http` callback at a
  number. Use `localhost` instead. It is the same server, by name.

So connect from app.recued.com, if you use it. Or open Recued on the server
at `http://localhost:7717/webclient`. Is this address new to your browser?
Then pair it once, like a new device. Does your server have no screen? Make a
tunnel from your own computer:

```sh
ssh -L 7717:127.0.0.1:7717 you@your-server
```

Then open `http://localhost:7717/webclient` on your computer. You only
connect once. After that, the account keeps working from any address.

Whoever makes the app follows these steps. For a work account, that is the
admin. With your own account, you need an Entra directory first. Sign up
for a free Azure account, and you get one.

1. Open the Azure portal. Go to **Microsoft Entra ID**, then
   **App registrations**, then **New registration**.
2. Under **Supported account types**, choose **Accounts in any
   organizational directory and personal Microsoft accounts**.
3. Under **Redirect URI**, pick **Web**. Paste the callback URL that Recued
   shows. It is on the **Microsoft** form under **Connections**. Then choose
   **Register**.
4. Open **API permissions**. Choose **Add a permission**, then
   **Microsoft Graph**, then **Delegated permissions**.
5. Add `Mail.Read`, `offline_access` and `User.Read`. Add `Mail.Send` if
   Recued should send mail. Add `Calendars.ReadWrite` for your calendar.
6. Open **Certificates & secrets**. Make a new client secret. Copy its
   **Value** right away. Azure shows it only once.
7. Copy the **Application (client) ID** from the **Overview** page.

Recued signs in through one shared address at Microsoft. So the other
account types fail. A personal account cannot use an app made for work
accounts only. No one can use an app made for just one workplace.

Leave out `offline_access`, and Recued cannot renew its sign-in. Syncing
would then stop about an hour after you connect.

This step is for a work or school account. The admin opens
**API permissions** on the app. There they choose **Grant admin consent**.

Without it, sign-in stops at "Need admin approval". Some workplaces show
"Approval required" instead. Send the request it offers. Then connect again
once an admin says yes.

A workplace needs only one app. All staff connect with the same Client ID and
secret. Each person pastes them into the **Microsoft** form in Recued.

The callback is the same for all of them too. The one on app.recued.com
never changes. On `localhost`, Microsoft ignores the port.

The secret names the app, not a person. It opens no mailbox by itself. Each
person still signs in with their own account. They only reach their own mail.

- [Connections](../guides/connections.md). How a saved connection works.
- [Connect Gmail and Google Calendar](connect-google.md). The same choices
  for a Google account.
- [Pairing and devices](pairing-and-devices.md). Pair a browser with your
  server.

The server is the product. It is a free program you run yourself. It runs
every recipe. It holds your warehouse and your secret keys. It writes the
audit record. It can run on a laptop or a home server. It can also run on a
supported single-board computer, or a small VPS. A VPS is a small server
you rent online. For scheduled and reactive work, choose a machine that
stays on.

This is the normal way to install. One command does it all. It fetches the
signed binary for your platform. It checks the release manifest against
Recued's pinned key. It checks the binary's signature and its declared
SHA-256. Only then does it install. It puts `recued` on your path. And it
sets the server to start when you log in.

On Linux or macOS, open a terminal and run:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://recued.com/install.sh | sh
```

On Windows, open PowerShell first. Press **Start**, type **PowerShell**, and
open it. Then paste:

```powershell
irm https://recued.com/install.ps1 | iex
```

It works on Linux and Windows on x64 or arm64. It works on macOS on Apple
Silicon and Intel. The macOS builds are signed and notarized with a
Developer ID. On Linux and macOS the script needs `curl`. It also needs
`jq` to read the release manifest. If `jq` is missing, the script tries to
install it, or tells you the exact command to run.

The script prints what to do next. A new server has to be set up once, by
pairing a client to it.

Start at login is on by default, and the script starts the server right
away. So it is already running. To pair:

1. Run `recued pair`. It prints a pairing code, the server's addresses, and
   the pairing link.
2. Pair the webclient or the Browser Bridge with that code. See
   [Pairing and devices](pairing-and-devices.md).

Nothing can pair with the server without a code. A code lasts 15 minutes.
Run `recued pair` again for a fresh one, or `recued pair --pair-code-ttl 24h`
for a longer window.

If you turned start at login off, or the script could not start the server,
start it yourself: run `recued serve`, or `recued` on Windows. It prints a
pairing code and the webclient link. That server runs only while its window
stays open.

Three things to know:

- If you seal the key file with a passphrase, the server starts locked. It
  waits for `recued unlock`. Sealed to the machine instead, it starts ready.
  See "Protecting the key file" below.
- On macOS, Windows, and a Linux desktop, start-at-login is set up for your
  user. No root is needed. Headless Linux needs root for a boot unit, so
  run the script with `sudo` there. Without root, a headless install sets up
  no autostart, and says so, rather than writing a unit that would fail on
  every boot.
- On macOS, never run the script with `sudo`. The server has to run as you.
  Run as root, it keeps its own realm, and a pairing code from your account
  never reaches it. The script refuses `sudo` on macOS. When you cannot write
  to `/usr/local`, it installs into `~/.local/lib/recued` and `~/.local/bin`
  instead, and adds that folder to your PATH for new terminals.

Put any of these just before `sh`, like this:
`curl -fsSL https://recued.com/install.sh | RECUED_AUTOSTART=0 sh`. Put it
before `curl` instead, and only `curl` sees it. The script then runs without
it. In PowerShell, run `$env:RECUED_AUTOSTART=0` on its own line first.

| Option | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `RECUED_AUTOSTART=0` | Do not start at login. Then the server runs only while you run it. An update cannot restart it for you |
| `RECUED_PREFIX` / `RECUED_BINDIR` | Where the program files and the `recued` command go. The defaults are `/usr/local/lib/recued` and `/usr/local/bin`. On macOS, when you cannot write those, the defaults are `~/.local/lib/recued` and `~/.local/bin`. On Linux, set both to install without `sudo`. On Windows the default is `%LOCALAPPDATA%\recued\bin` |
| `RECUED_NO_MODIFY_PATH=1` | Do not add the command's folder to your shell's profile. By default, when that folder is not on your PATH, the script adds it for new terminals |
| `RECUED_CHANNEL=edge` | Follow the edge channel instead of stable |
| `RECUED_FORCE=1` | Install again, even when you already have the released version |

Run the script again at any time. It updates a server that is behind. It
repairs a broken install. On a server that is already current, it changes
nothing unless you pass `RECUED_FORCE=1`. It does not restart a server that
is running. It prints the restart command for your system instead. To
uninstall, stop the running server first. The script prints the exact
commands for that too.

The script is the normal path. The other paths are for contributors, and
for people who want to download by hand. Get the server from the current
release page. Take the signed binary. Is there no verified file for your
platform? Then you cannot get that release channel there. Do not skip the
signature check.

| Path | Best for | Update owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Install script | Most people. A Mac, Windows, or Linux machine you look after | The script installs and updates. The server can also stage signed releases on its chosen channel |
| Binary, by hand | The same machines, when you cannot run the script | The server can stage signed releases on its chosen channel |
| From source | Contributors and custom builds | You rebuild. The server only reports that a release exists |

All paths run the same server. The choice changes how it is packed and
updated. It does not change how recipes behave. It does not change how
grants work, or where your data lives. See [Updates](updates.md) for
channels, and for how a server applies a release safely.

The install script does all of this for you. Do it by hand only when you
cannot run the script. Download the file for your operating system and CPU
from the signed release. The installer checks three things. It checks the
release manifest. It checks the binary's signature. It checks the declared
SHA-256. After that it puts `recued` on your path. If a check fails, the
installer stops. Do not go on.

To keep a foreground server and its data together while you test:

```sh
mkdir -p ./recued-data
recued serve --db ./recued-data/recued.db
```

The start-up banner shows the real database path. It shows the local URL.
And it shows the first pairing code. For an always-on install, run the same
command under your system's service manager. Do not rely on an open
terminal window.

You can build the same server from a source checkout. You need Node.js 20
or newer, and npm:

```sh
npm install
npm --workspace @recued/server run build
mkdir -p ./recued-data
node backend/server/dist/bin.js serve --db ./recued-data/recued.db
```

Run those commands from the top folder of the checkout. Source builds use
the `source` update channel. They can tell you a newer release exists. They
never replace your build by themselves.

All the server knows lives in its data directory. That means the warehouse
database and the files stored by content hash. It also means the connection
records and the installed recipes. And it means the update ledger and the
audit history. Treat that directory as who the server is:

- Put it on storage that survives a restart or an upgrade.
- Let only the account that runs Recued use it. It holds encrypted secrets
  and working details. That is true even after encryption at rest is on.
- Back it up like anything you cannot download again. There is no hosted
  Recued copy to restore from.
- Keep the recovery key from the first pairing away from the machine. The
  server unlocks with its local key file. The recovery key is the other way
  back into the same encrypted state.

The backup we support is the one-file encrypted archive. Read
[Backup and restore](backup-and-restore.md). Copying a live database
directory is not the same as an archive. It only works if your platform
can take a snapshot all at once.

The key file sits in the data directory. So decide what protects it before
the first start. The server seals it with the first factor it can find:

| Factor | When it applies | Where the secret lives |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `RECUED_IDENTITY_PASSPHRASE` | You set the variable | Your environment or a secret manager |
| A platform secret store | The macOS login keychain, Windows DPAPI, or systemd-creds can hold a secret for this host | The platform store, outside the data directory |
| Unsealed | Neither of the above can be used | Nothing. The key file can be read right next to the database |

Set the passphrase before you start the server for the first time:

```sh
export RECUED_IDENTITY_PASSPHRASE='a long, random passphrase'
recued serve --db ./recued-data/recued.db
```

Keep it in the thing that starts the server. That could be a systemd
`EnvironmentFile`, a compose `env_file`, or a secret manager. Do not put it
in the config file. That file lives in the very directory the passphrase
protects. Once a key file is sealed with a passphrase, the server needs
the passphrase at every start. With no passphrase, the server
stops with a clear error. It does not start without it.

Changing the passphrase later is cheap. Stop the server and run:

```sh
recued rotate-passphrase --db ./recued-data/recued.db
```

It seals the same key file again under the new passphrase. The realm, the
data, and the server identity stay the same. Nothing has to pair again. Put
the new value in the service's environment before you start the server.

Changing which *factor* seals the key file is a bigger deal. That choice is
saved when the file is made. It stays that way for good, for that realm.

Before the first pairing, the key file is throwaway. Changing your mind
costs a fresh identity and nothing more. Stop the server. Delete the key
file. Set or unset the variable. Start again.

After the first pairing, it costs more. You must make the server identity
again. That takes `recued recover-keyfile` and your recovery key. Then
every paired device must pair again. The publisher identity changes. The
account binding is lost. The data itself is not touched.

An unsealed server still works. Its warehouse is still encrypted. Sealing
adds one thing. A copy of the whole data directory does not carry the key
that opens it. Run `recued auth-status` at any time to see which factor is
in use.

`recued status` should say the server is running. From the same machine,
check the health address. It needs no login:

```sh
curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:7717/health
```

A healthy server answers with HTTP 200 and a JSON body that contains
`"status":"ok"`. That proves the program is taking requests. It does not
prove a connection or a recipe works. Next, read the running server's
start-up log. It shows the addresses it can be reached on. It shows the
webclient link and the pairing code. For a start-at-login install, use
your system's log viewer. Or run `recued pair`. It
prints a fresh code, the server's addresses, and the pairing link.

The code works once. It stops working after 15 minutes. Did it run out
before the first pairing? Run `recued pair` for a new one. Or restart the
server with the same database and the same settings, and read the new code
from its start-up log. A
server is not ready to pair if it cannot write its data directory. The same
is true if it cannot open its port, or cannot print a pairing code. Fix that
first.

A server that only your own network can reach is a fully working server.
Keep it on loopback or a private network unless some other device needs
it. Public reach matters only for features that get traffic from outside.
Read [Reachability](reachability.md) before you open firewall ports, DNS,
or certificates.
Attach a client in [Pairing and devices](pairing-and-devices.md).

Your server listens on two ports. Each one reaches a different place.

| Port | Reaches | Needs a certificate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 7717 | The computer running the server | No |
| 443 | Any device, at home or away | Yes |

Port 7717 works as soon as the server starts. Open this on that same
computer:

```
http://127.0.0.1:7717/webclient/
```

That page is served by your own server. Nothing else is needed.

A browser only runs Recued from a safe address. An `https` address is
safe. A plain `http` address is not.

There is one exception. Your browser trusts `127.0.0.1`. That address can
only mean the computer you are sitting at.

Your phone cannot use it. Your phone needs a real `https` address. That
means a certificate.

One more thing is worth knowing. Port 443 serves both the visitor page and
the app. So you only ever open one port.

section: Three free ways to get a certificate
body:
### Tailscale

Tailscale builds a small private network across your devices. It hands out
real certificates. It needs no open ports at all.

Install it on your server and on your phone. Then run this on the server:

```
tailscale cert my-server.my-tailnet.ts.net
tailscale serve --bg https / http://127.0.0.1:7717
```

Now open that same name on your phone. It works at home and away.

### Caddy

Caddy is a small web server. It fetches and renews certificates for you.
You need a domain name for this one.

Put this in a file called `Caddyfile`:

```
recued.example.com {
	reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:7717
}
```

Then run `caddy run`. Point your domain at your home address first.

### A certificate you already have

Some people already own a domain and a certificate. Upload it under
Settings, then Server, then Certificates.

| You have | Pick |
| --- | --- |
| No domain name | Tailscale |
| A domain name | Caddy |
| A domain and a certificate | Upload it |

Recued Pro does this step for you. It gives the server a name. It keeps
the certificate fresh. You still open one router port, as below.

At home a certificate is enough. Away from home there is one more step.
Your router has to let port 443 through to your server.

Tailscale is the exception. It needs no router change at all.

You cannot see the answer from inside your own network. Recued can ask
from outside instead. Open Settings, then Server, then Connect a device.
The router step there has a button called Check this now.

A check that gets in ticks the step. A check that does not tells you to
open your router settings. If nothing has checked yet, the step says so
rather than guessing.

Pairing links a client to your server. A client is a device or app that
shows you things and does what your server tells it. Clients never run
recipes. They never hold your warehouse or your account secret keys. Pairing
goes straight from the client to your server. The cloud is not part of it.

The webclient is a thin app at `app.recued.com`. Your server also serves
its own copy at `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/webclient/`. That is the address
the start-up log prints. On the server machine, that copy pairs with no
certificate and no internet. To reach it from another device on your
network, see [Reachability](reachability.md). To pair:

1. Read the address and the single-use code from the running server's
   start-up log.
2. Open the webclient. Enter the server address. On a fresh server, also
   enter the pairing code.
3. Complete the recovery-key steps.
4. Compare the server identity shown on both sides. If they match, accept.

The first pairing code stops working after 15 minutes. Did it run out? Run
`recued pair` on the server machine. It prints a fresh code, the server's
addresses, and the pairing link. The running server accepts that code.
Need a longer window? Run `recued pair --pair-code-ttl 24h`. Restarting the
server with the same database and settings also prints a new code in its
start-up log.

Pairing gives the client a limited pass. You can cancel that pass any
time. Pairing does not move your data.

The recovery key is 24 secret words. It does two jobs. First, it lets you
link clients to your server. Second, from the first pairing on, it can
restore the data your server encrypts. Here is why. The first pairing turns
on encryption for data at rest. After that, the server unlocks itself at
each start from its own key file. The recovery key is the only other thing
that can unwrap the same master key.

Store the recovery key offline. Do not keep it only on the machine it
protects. Anyone who has it can pair a client. If you lose both it and
the server's key file, the encrypted data cannot be recovered.
The same 24 words open your backup archives. See
[Backup and restore](backup-and-restore.md).

The Browser Bridge is a browser extension. Its job is small on purpose. It
watches for page triggers a recipe declared. It reads pages and does
actions on live websites. And it shows operating-system notifications. It
does all of this for your server. It runs only signed commands from your
server. It holds no engine state.

Install the extension. Pair it the same way as the webclient. You only need
a Bridge for two kinds of recipe. One kind watches or acts on a live web
page. The other sends an operating-system notification through the Bridge.
Everything else runs without one. A recipe that needs a Bridge says so before it runs. It does
not fail halfway.

Every paired client listens to the server's live broadcast. That carries
run progress, approvals, warehouse changes, and schedule state. The client
shows it as it happens. The broadcast carries state to the client's screen.
The server stays in charge of that state.

The Devices page lists every paired client. Revoke any entry to cancel that
client's pass right away. Pair again later and it gets a fresh pass. Revoke a
Bridge, and recipes that need it stop doing page actions until a Bridge is
paired again.

Decide whether your server needs a public name in
[Reachability](reachability.md).

Reachability means: can other computers find your server? A Recued server
works fully on your own network. Only some features need traffic to come
in from the internet. When you do give your server a public name, that
name points straight at your server. The cloud publishes the name. It can
also issue the certificate. But it is not in the path of your traffic. It
cannot read what flows to you.

| Feature | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Webclient away from your network | Your browser must reach the server |
| External AI agents over MCP | The agent's machine must reach the server |
| Slack and Telegram triggers | The chat platforms send messages straight to your server |
| Vendor webhooks | Providers such as HubSpot send events over HTTPS |
| Public endpoint pages | Visitors load forms and pages your server hosts |

Outbound-only integrations need none of this. IMAP mail sync, API polling,
and Salesforce's streaming subscription are all connections your server
opens outward. Some vendors can only push webhooks. If your server has no
public URL, those vendors fall back to a regular check.

Getting a public name is really three choices. They do not depend on each
other:

1. **Which name?** A domain you already own, or a `<handle>.recued.net` name
   that Recued gives you.
2. **Who keeps the certificate current?** You, or Recued.
3. **Can traffic get in?** Only you can answer that one. It is the router
   step below, and nothing buys your way out of it.

Pro changes only the second answer. Your own domain works either way. That
is the part worth being clear about, because the upkeep is very different.

| Your setup | Certificate | What you do afterwards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Your domain, TLS ends at a proxy in front | Recued never holds one | Nothing. Your proxy renews it |
| Your domain, certificate uploaded to Recued | You get it | **Upload a new one about every 90 days.** Recued serves an uploaded certificate but does not renew it |
| Your domain, **with Pro** | Recued issues and renews it | Nothing, once two DNS records exist |
| `<handle>.recued.net`, **with Pro** | Recued issues and renews it | Nothing |

Everything except the Pro rows is free forever. Pro unlocks no feature. On
every row, your traffic goes straight to your server.

The middle row used to make paying customers worse off. Bring your own
domain, and you were back to a certificate chore every 90 days. Meanwhile
the `recued.net` name renewed itself. Now Pro covers your own domain on the
same terms.

A name and a certificate are not enough on their own. The name points at
your home. Your router still has to pass that traffic to your server.

So let port 443 through your router, to the machine running Recued. You do
this once, in your router's own settings. Recued cannot do it for you, and
neither can the cloud. Your traffic never goes through the cloud, which is
the point of the design and the reason this step is yours.

**Pro does not change this.** Pro gives you the name and the certificate.
The router step stays yours either way.

Tailscale is the exception. It links your devices privately, so no router
change is needed at all. See
[Use Recued on another device](lan-access.md).

You cannot check this from inside your own network. A request from your own
house may never reach the router's outside. Open **Settings → Server →
Connect a device**. The router step there has a button called Check this
now. It asks from outside and tells you what it found.

section: How the name and certificate work
body:
