Most home and small-VPS addresses change over time. Dynamic DNS solves
that. Your server keeps its own name record pointed at its current address.
So the name always works. It points straight at your server, with no proxy
in between. The certificate is what makes the name trusted. It is issued
through an ACME DNS challenge. The private key is made and kept on your
server. The cloud handles two things: the name record and the challenge.
It sees your hostname and your public IP. It sees none of your traffic.
You can run all of this yourself, with your own domain, DNS, and
certificate tools. The mechanics are the same.

Point the name at your server. Handle TLS yourself. There are two shapes.

**End TLS in front of Recued.** Use a reverse proxy, Caddy, or anything else
that holds the certificate and forwards to your server. Recued never sees a
certificate. Your proxy renews it on its own schedule. Register the
hostname in **Settings → Server → Hostnames** as *Handled outside Recued*.
Then the server knows the name is yours, and expects TLS to arrive already
handled.

**Upload the certificate to Recued.** Get one however you like: certbot,
your registrar, your employer's PKI. Upload it in **Settings → Server →
TLS Certificates**. Recued serves it for that hostname.

⚠ Recued does **not** renew a certificate you upload. It cannot get a new
one for you. It uses the one you gave it until that one runs out. It warns
you as the end gets close. Plan to upload a new one about every 90 days. Or
pick one of the other two paths.

Recued issues and renews the certificate for a domain you own. You create
two DNS records, once. The second one does the real work.

You can use your root domain, like `your-domain.com`. Or you can use a
subdomain, like `recued.your-domain.com`. Both work. Most people want the
root domain. So this page shows that path first, with Cloudflare as the
example. The subdomain path comes after it.

The first record makes your domain reach your server. The second lets
Recued prove it may issue certificates for that name.

You need both. Having only the first fails in a confusing way. Your domain
finds your server. Your server answers. But no certificate can ever be
issued. Certificates are checked against a different name: your hostname
with `_acme-challenge.` in front. For the root domain, that is
`_acme-challenge.your-domain.com`. That name is in a zone Recued cannot
write to. The second record points it at a zone Recued *can* write to. The
certificate authority follows it.

**Settings → Server → Hostnames** fills in both records with your own
handle. It checks them live. It tells you which one is wrong.

These are the two records for a root domain:

| | Name | Type | Value |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Routing | `your-domain.com` (`@`) | ALIAS / ANAME / flattened CNAME | `<handle>.recued.net` |
| Certificates | `_acme-challenge.your-domain.com` | CNAME | `_acme-challenge.<handle>.recued.net` |

DNS forbids a plain CNAME at the root of a zone. So the routing record uses
your provider's ALIAS, ANAME, or CNAME-flattening option instead. That is a
record type that acts like a CNAME but answers with addresses. That is
allowed at a root. Cloudflare, Route 53, DNSimple, and deSEC all have one,
under one of those three names.

⚠ **Only the routing record is special.** The second record is still a
plain CNAME. That is because `_acme-challenge.your-domain.com` is a
*subdomain* of your root. It is not the root itself. The CNAME rule does not
reach it. No ALIAS is needed. This is the step most people over-think.

section: Cloudflare, step 1: add the two records
body:
Your domain's nameservers must be at Cloudflare. If your domain lives
somewhere else, you can move just its DNS to Cloudflare. A free plan is
enough. Or use your own provider's ALIAS or ANAME record instead.

1. Sign in to Cloudflare and pick your domain. Open **DNS → Records**.
2. Does `@` (your root) already have an `A` or `AAAA` record? That could be
   an old site or a parked page. Delete it first. A name cannot hold a CNAME
   and an address record at the same time.
3. Click **Add record** for the routing record. Type: **CNAME**. Name: `@`.
   Target: `<handle>.recued.net`. Proxy status: **DNS only** (click the
   orange cloud so it turns grey). TTL: **Auto**. Save.
4. Click **Add record** again for the certificate record. Type: **CNAME**.
   Name: `_acme-challenge`. Target: `_acme-challenge.<handle>.recued.net`.
   Proxy status: **DNS only**. TTL: **Auto**. Save.
5. Look at both rows. Both clouds must be grey and say "DNS only". Cloudflare
   turns the orange cloud on by default for a new record. An orange cloud
   breaks both records. See "proxying hides the record" below.

Cloudflare allows a CNAME at the root because it flattens it for you. It
answers with addresses, which DNS allows at a root. And it looks up
`<handle>.recued.net` again each time. So it follows your server when the
address changes.

section: Cloudflare, step 2: check it in Recued
body:
1. Open **Settings → Server → Hostnames**. Add `your-domain.com`. For the
   certificate, pick **My own domain, managed by Recued**.
2. Use **Verify** on its row to prove you own the domain. Pick **DNS TXT**
   or **HTTP token**. The panel shows what to add. A TXT record in
   Cloudflare must be **DNS only** too.
3. The panel shows both records with your real handle filled in. It shows
   the short names (`@` and `_acme-challenge`) and the full names.
4. Run the DNS check. It has three parts. **Your domain points at this
   server** stays a warning (⚠) on a root domain. That is normal. The next
   sections say why. **Certificate delegation** must pass. **Certificate
   authority permissions (CAA)** passes if you have no CAA records, or if
   they allow all three authorities. See Limits below.
5. Did a part fail? The panel names the record to fix. Fix it in Cloudflare,
   then run the check again. Cloudflare changes usually show up within a few
   minutes.

Want `www.your-domain.com` too? See "Using both the root and `www`" below.

This path has no catches. Any DNS provider can do it. Both records are
plain CNAMEs.

| | Name | Type | Value |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Routing | `recued.your-domain.com` | CNAME | `<handle>.recued.net` |
| Certificates | `_acme-challenge.recued.your-domain.com` | CNAME | `_acme-challenge.<handle>.recued.net` |

In Cloudflare the steps are the same as above, with two changes. The
routing record's Name is `recued`, not `@`. The certificate record's Name is
`_acme-challenge.recued`. Both stay **DNS only**.

The first label is yours to pick: `recued`, `home`, `hq`, anything. Nothing
in Recued reads it.

section: What to expect on a root domain
body:
Two things are normal on a root domain. The routing check stays a warning.
And you must never type an address in by hand. The next sections explain
both.

section: The routing check stays a warning
body:
Once a flattened record is in place, the Hostnames panel reports the
routing check as a warning, not a pass:

> Resolves to the right address today, but as a flattened A record rather than
> a CNAME — if your provider does not keep it in sync with your Recued address,
> it will break when your IP changes.

That is the normal steady state for a root domain. It is a warning, not a
pass, for a reason. DNS cannot tell Recued the difference between two
things. One is a provider that re-flattens on every change. The other is
an address someone typed in once. It does not block anything. Issuing a certificate depends on
the `_acme-challenge` record and your CAA records. It never depends on the
routing record.

section: Do not pin an address by hand
body:
There is one way to get a root domain wrong. You look up your server's
current address. You type it in as an `A` record. That works until the
address changes. Then the name points at somebody else's machine. That is
the exact failure dynamic DNS exists to prevent. Recued reports it as
*"Points at an address that is no longer yours"*. But only once it has
already happened.

Use ALIAS, ANAME, or flattening instead. Then your provider looks up
`<handle>.recued.net` again by itself.

section: If your provider has no ALIAS option
body:
Some registrars' bundled DNS has none. Cloudflare has one: it flattens a
CNAME at the root by itself. Two ways out, best first:

- **Move DNS for the domain** to a provider that has one. Your registration
  stays where it is. Only the nameservers change.
- **Use a subdomain instead.** `recued.your-domain.com` needs nothing
  special. It works on every provider.

A root-domain redirect service is not a way out. It answers HTTP. Recued
needs the name itself to point at your server.

They are two hostnames. Enrol each one in **Settings → Server → Hostnames**.
Give each its own pair of records: a flattened routing record at the root,
and a plain CNAME at `www`. Add an `_acme-challenge` CNAME for each. Each
gets its own certificate. Each counts on its own against the five-domain
limit below.

section: Getting the records right: names are relative
body:
Most DNS providers want the name relative to your zone. So enter
`_acme-challenge.recued`, not the full
`_acme-challenge.recued.your-domain.com`. If you paste the full name, you
usually get `_acme-challenge.recued.your-domain.com.your-domain.com`. Nobody
complains. The record looks made, and it points nowhere. On a root domain,
the routing record's relative name is `@`. Its challenge record's relative
name is `_acme-challenge`. The Hostnames panel shows both the relative and
the full form of every record, for this very reason.

section: Getting the records right: proxying hides the record
body:
Some providers can proxy a record. In Cloudflare that is the orange cloud.
Both records must be set to "DNS only". A proxied CNAME is answered with
the provider's own addresses instead. So the certificate authority cannot
follow the `_acme-challenge` one. And a proxied routing record puts that
provider in the path of your traffic. TLS ends there. That is the very
thing the rest of this page exists to avoid. Cloudflare proxies by default.
So this is the common case, not a rare one. On a root domain it is easy to
miss, because Cloudflare's flattening and its proxy are separate settings
on the same record.

A trailing dot on a value is fine either way. Providers differ, and both
spellings are accepted.

It is not a one-time step. Every renewal uses it. Delete it, and nothing
breaks today. Everything breaks about 60 days from now, when the
certificate runs out.

Recued checks the record again on a schedule. It does not wait for a
renewal to fail. It flags the hostname as soon as the record stops working.
Quietly, when there is plenty of certificate time left. Urgently, as the
end gets close.

Up to five custom domains per server. This part is Pro. It uses Recued's
certificate-issuing capacity on your behalf. Each domain gets its own
certificate. They do not share one. So a mistake in your zone can never
affect your `<handle>.recued.net` name. That is the address you would need
in order to come back and fix things.

CAA records can limit which authorities may issue for your domain. If you
have them, add all three: `sectigo.com`, `pki.goog`, and `letsencrypt.org`.
Recued rotates between them. Allow only some of them, and you get a
certificate that renews most of the time. That is the worst kind of failure
to find. CAA is inherited down the tree. A record set at your root applies
to a subdomain too. So check, even when the name you enroll has none of
its own.

Browsers only allow the cryptography that pairing and the webclient need
in a secure context. That means HTTPS, or plain HTTP on a loopback address.
This is why the start-up log prints `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/webclient/`.
On the server machine itself, that address needs no certificate. It works
offline.

section: Reaching the webclient from another device
body:
Your server answers on every network interface. So
`http://192.168.1.x:<port>/webclient/` loads from a phone or laptop on the
same network. The page appears. Then the app stops with a message instead
of pairing. Nothing is broken. A plain-HTTP address on a LAN IP is not a
secure context. So the browser holds back the Web Crypto APIs pairing
needs. Recued says so, instead of failing in a confusing way.

Two ways forward:

**Put HTTPS in front.** Anything that handles TLS works. It can be a
reverse proxy with a certificate. It can be a private-network service that
provides one. Or it can be a name and certificate as described above. This
is the lasting answer. It is the only
one that scales past a single device.

**Opt one browser in.** Chromium browsers can treat one specific origin as
secure. Open `chrome://flags/#unsafely-treat-insecure-origin-as-secure`.
Add the exact origin, such as `http://192.168.1.121:7718`, with matching
host and port. Restart the browser. This is per device and per browser. It
relaxes a protection for that origin in general. That is reasonable on a
home network you control. It is not something to hand to other people.

section: Choose which address the server binds
body:
By default the server detects your network interface. It binds every
interface. So it can be reached on loopback and on your LAN address. Some
machines have several candidate interfaces, such as a container bridge or
a VM network next to the real one. Then the server follows your default
route to decide which address to publish.

To pin it, set `network.lan_bind_address` in `config.toml` and restart:

```toml
[runtime]
"network.lan_bind_address" = "192.168.1.121"
```

The value is bound exactly as written. So it also narrows what the server
answers on. `127.0.0.1` serves only the server machine. `0.0.0.0` serves
everything. If the address is not one this machine has, the server logs
the reason at start-up. Then it falls back to detection. It does not refuse
to start.
Pick a release channel in [Updates](updates.md).

This page lists the problems people really hit. It starts from what you
see. Every fix has the same shape: what you see, why it happens, what to
do.

**Pairing fails in the browser on a LAN address.** Browsers only allow the
cryptography pairing needs in a secure context. So `http://192.168.x.x`
fails on purpose. Pair over HTTPS. Or pair over `localhost` on the server
machine itself. See [Reachability](reachability.md).

**A new pairing code is rejected right away.** A code works once, and only
for 15 minutes. Get a fresh one with `recued pair` on the server machine.
It prints the code, the server's addresses, and the pairing link. The
running server accepts it. Use the code that was printed last: a new code
replaces the old one. A code from a different server, or from a different
database, is not this server's code.

**The webclient looks signed in but nothing loads.** The client shows the
last thing it knew, even when it cannot reach the server. After a server
restart or a network change, give it a moment. Then reload. If it still
sticks, check that the server is running and can be reached.

**A recipe that watches or touches a live page refuses to run.** Page
triggers, page reads, and page actions need a paired Browser Bridge. The
recipe says so before it runs. It does not fail halfway. Pair a Bridge. Or
leave that recipe for a machine that has one.

**A reactive recipe stopped firing.** After it fails several times in a
row, the circuit breaker turns the recipe off and tells you. That is on
purpose. Fix the cause. Maybe a connection is missing, or an AI step cannot
be served. Then turn the recipe on again. It never turns itself back on.

**A watcher seems to do nothing.** Quiet ticks are silent on purpose. When
a trigger step returns `should_run: false`, the tick leaves no audit entry
and no output. Silence means "nothing matched". It does not mean "broken".

**A condition never matches.** The most common cause is quotes around a
value. `equal 'closed_won'` compares against the quotes too, so it never
matches. Values in condition strings are always bare: `equal closed_won`.

**A guard halts a run you expected to pass.** A guard halts when its
condition is **met**. So `"guard": "{{step.deal}} is_null"` stops the run
when the deal is missing. Read it as "stop if". Do not read it as "require
that".

**An AI step fails before the recipe starts.** The preflight check matched
every AI step against your set-up sources. It found no fit. Each source
that cannot be used has a reason. Maybe there is no key. Maybe its
limit is used up. Maybe it is turned off. Or maybe it cannot do what the
step asks. The fix is in **Settings → AI/Models**. Add a source, or ask for
less in the step.

**An embedding producer says no embeddings model is set up.** Normal AI
sources cannot do vector work. Set up the special slot under
**Settings → AI/Models → Providers → Embeddings**. Embedding calls use only
that slot. They do not fall back to the free pool or to the fast and
quality slots.

**Background enrichment never runs.** Three switches control it. First, the
topic's trust level. Off stays off, and manual stays manual. Nothing turns
itself up. Second, the global Pause-AI window. Third, the topic's pool
policy. Free-only stalls when the free pool is used up. Check them in that
order.

**A vendor capability shows "disabled" after enrollment.** The provider
gave less than the pack needs. Maybe a HubSpot scope is missing. Maybe the
Salesforce user profile cannot see an object. Grant it again in your own
vendor app, or fix the Salesforce profile. Then enroll again. The warning
names what is missing.

**CRM data lags behind the vendor.** Without a public URL, your server
cannot receive vendor webhooks. So it falls back to a regular check against
the vendor. The data still arrives, on that schedule. Give the server a
public name to get changes at event speed. Salesforce is the exception. Its
streaming subscription goes outward, so it works without a public name.

**A connection keeps failing after working for months.** On an auth
failure, one automatic token refresh is tried. If it keeps failing, the
grant itself has most likely been revoked or has expired at the provider.
Enroll the connection again under the same name. The recipes that depend
on it carry on unchanged.

**A recipe reports its connection is not bound.** The recipe's connection
picker was never given a real connection on this install. Open the
recipe's configuration and pick one. If the list is empty, enroll one
first.

**Restore refuses with "target not empty".** The restore that runs before
pairing only targets fresh servers. That is on purpose. It will not write
over a server that already has data. On a server in use, restore from
**Settings → Backup & Recovery** instead. That path has its own guards.

**Restore refuses with "archive too new".** The archive was exported by a
newer server version than the one restoring it. Update the server first.
Then restore. The other way round works by itself: an older archive moves
forward on a newer server.

**Wrong recovery key during restore.** It bounces cleanly. Nothing is
saved. The server stays untouched. Send the right key and it carries on.
You do not upload the archive again.

**The server did not come back after a restore.** The save ends in a
restart. Installs with a supervisor come back by themselves. The start-at-login
setup the install script makes is one. A server running in a plain
terminal window needs starting again by hand.

**An update seemed to apply, then the old version is running.** The
start-up health check failed. So the server went back by itself. That is
the safety working. It is not a failed rollback. Check the server logs for
what broke before you try again. The attempt is written in the update
ledger.

An update is a new version of the server program. Your server can update
itself while nobody is watching. It is built so it can never break itself
quietly. And it never tells anyone who it is when it checks.

A channel is the line of releases your server follows.

| Channel | Who it is for |
| --- | --- |
| `stable` | The default. Releases that have settled. |
| `edge` | Early releases, for people who want changes first. |

A release can go out to a share of servers at a time. Your server works
out by itself, on your own machine, whether it is in that share. The update
check sends no account name, no handle, and no install identity. Nothing
says who you are.

A manifest is a signed list that describes one release. It names the files,
their digests, and when the list expires. A digest is like a fingerprint
for a file. Your server checks the chain of signatures before it stages
anything. An old list is refused. A copy of an old list sent again is
refused too.

section: How each install path applies updates
body:
- **Binary** — it downloads the new version, checks it, swaps itself, then
  restarts.
- **From source** — you get a note that a release exists. Building it is up
  to you.

An update happens in two steps. First the new version is staged and
started. Then it must pass a start-up health check. Only then is it kept.
If the check fails, the server goes back to the old version by itself.

Some releases change the database. Those take a snapshot first, before the
change. Going back to a version from before that change is refused. That
keeps your data safe.

One lock on the whole machine stops two update paths from running at once.
Every try is written to an update ledger. The ledger only grows. It is kept
outside the database it talks about.

Only the server owner controls updates. Connected AI agents cannot see the
update controls. No cloud service can push an update onto your server. Your
server pulls the update, checks it, and decides.

See how permission works in
[Grants and approvals](../concepts/grants-and-approvals.md).
